4.label: Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef
4.bio: One of the greatest Tannaim, he shaped the world of the Oral Torah after the destruction of the Temple, leading a broken generation with love of Israel and self-sacrifice.
4.core_concept: The Torah as a revolutionary national act, uniting inner depth with public struggle.

41.label: Maimonides (Rambam)
41.bio: A double revolutionary — he codified halakha with clarity, closing the era of the Talmud, while at the same time formulating a rational faith in the Guide for the Perplexed.
41.core_concept: Order, reason, fundamental principles of faith. The Torah is built on knowledge – and leads to the redemption of the individual and the community.

44.label: Nahmanides (Ramban)
44.bio: Halakhic authority, commentator and kabbalist who wove together every layer of Torah, renewed the Jewish settlement of Jerusalem, and stood courageously before the Church.
44.core_concept: Combining plain sense, homily, mystery and kabbalistic interpretation – seeing nature as a series of hidden miracles.

33.label: Rabbenu Tam (R. Yaakov ben Meir) — architect of the Tosafist method
33.bio: Rashi's grandson, who built the method of the Tosafists: contradictions are not abandoned — passages are bridged and reconciled. He also led the community through the era of the Crusades and enacted far-reaching social ordinances.
33.core_concept: Strict loyalty to the text of the Gemara ("let nothing be erased from the books") that forces depth, precision and distinctions – and produces creative study.

72.label: The Maharal of Prague — the philosopher who joined intellect and mystery
72.bio: A central thinker who built a comprehensive system upon opposites, unity, and the reading of Midrash as a world of ideas. His influence is evident in Hasidism and among its opponents alike.
72.core_concept: A philosophical-midrashic language that gives depth to aggadah and Torah, and educates towards orderly, clear study.

127.label: The Chofetz Chaim (Rabbi Yisrael Meir HaKohen)
127.bio: Author of the Mishnah Berurah and Chofetz Chaim. He fused practical halakhic ruling with halakhic ethics, becoming a formative moral figure of the modern era.
127.core_concept: Making ethics binding halakha. Practical holiness that begins with speech.

443.label: Rabbi Yosef Karo
443.bio: Author of the Shulchan Aruch and one of the greatest halakhic codifiers, who shaped Jewish law in the generations after the expulsion from Spain.
443.core_concept: Creating order and halakhic unity for a scattered people.

134.label: Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook — the vision that united sacred and secular
134.bio: Rav Kook saw modernity as a divine process and secular Zionism as a profound movement of return. He sought unity between opposites, spoke in terms of development, and exercised halakhic-national leadership with responsibility for the Yishuv.
134.core_concept: The truth is revealed in the tension between opposites: "the old will be renewed and the new will be sanctified" – uniting forces instead of erasing them.

344.label: Rav Saadia Gaon
344.bio: One of the greatest of the Geonim, defender of the Oral Torah and founder of systematic Jewish philosophy.
344.core_concept: Bringing together faith, reason and tradition.

22.label: Rabbenu Gershom, Light of the Exile
22.bio: Leader of Ashkenazi Jewry, social legislator and liturgical poet. He enacted bold ordinances and established an independent Torah center in Europe.
22.core_concept: Torah with ethics: protecting the dignity of women, personal privacy, humanity towards forced converts.

25.label: Rav Hai Gaon
25.bio: A supreme halakhic authority to whom questions were sent from every Jewish diaspora. He wrote hundreds of responsa, halakhic monographs, a Hebrew-Aramaic lexicon, and liturgical poems.
25.core_concept: Establishing halakha as a binding foundation alongside aggadah as inspiration; building a literary bridge to the age of the Rishonim and making the Bavli the "book of law".

395.label: The Rashba (Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet)
395.bio: One of the greatest halakhic authorities and leaders of Spanish Jewry, a cornerstone of halakhic ruling for all generations.
395.core_concept: A balance between tradition, public leadership and scholarly depth.

276.label: The Rashbam
276.bio: Rashi's eldest grandson and one of the great Tosafists, whose Torah commentary emphasized the plain meaning of the text and its linguistic and narrative context.
276.core_concept: Illuminating the plain sense of Scripture as an independent layer within the wholeness of the Torah, without detracting from the force of the Oral Torah.

389.label: Deborah the Prophetess
389.bio: Prophetess and judge who sat beneath the palm of Deborah. Led Israel in the war against Sisera and sang the song of victory.
389.core_concept: Leadership out of mission, responsibility and faith.

sup-3.label: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
sup-3.bio: Savior of Torah in the generation of the destruction. Escaped besieged Jerusalem and asked 'Give me Yavneh and its sages' — securing the continuity of the Oral Torah after the Temple fell.

sup-4.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sup-4.bio: Redactor of the Mishnah and closer of the Tannaitic era. United the traditions of the Oral Torah into one authoritative work, combining Torah greatness with wealth and leadership before Rome.

sup-5.label: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki)
sup-5.bio: The foremost commentator of Israel. His commentary on the Torah and Talmud — clear, concise and faithful to the plain meaning — opened the gates of learning for all generations; no page of Talmud is studied without him.

sup-6.label: The Baal Shem Tov (Rabbi Yisrael Besht)
sup-6.bio: Founder of the Hasidic movement. Taught that no place is empty of God, placing devekut, joy and love of every Jew at the center of divine service — transforming Eastern European Jewry.

262.label: Rabbi Ephraim of Qal'at Hammad
262.bio: One of the profound figures between the age of the Geonim and the Rishonim of Spain and Provence, a "student-colleague" of the Rif. His glosses were absorbed into the Book of Halakhot, and he brought philological and grammatical sensitivity into halakhic ruling.
262.core_concept: Bringing linguistic precision and textual criticism in as essential halakhic tools, out of loyalty to tradition and intellectual courage.

47.label: The Maharam of Rothenburg
47.bio: Supreme halakhic authority and head of the Ashkenazi communities, who gave up his life so as not to endanger the public. His rulings shaped generations of Ashkenazi halakha.
47.core_concept: Halakhic responsibility that does not fear personal sacrifice. Ruling from fundamental principles, even at a heavy personal price.

463.label: The Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles)
463.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of Ashkenaz, who added his glosses to the Shulchan Arukh and made it the unifying halakhic code of all Israel.
463.core_concept: Custom is a living part of the halakhic tradition.

195.label: The Ra'avad of Posquières
195.bio: A central halakhic authority and author of the critical glosses on the Mishneh Torah; one of the key figures from whom Provençal Kabbalah grew.
195.core_concept: Halakha is a living conversation between sages, not a closed code.

13.label: The Ran (Rabbenu Nissim of Girona)
13.bio: A halakhic authority and leader in an age of crisis who combined rationality with original Torah thought; founder of a dual conception of law.
13.core_concept: A distinction between the ideal law of the Torah and the pragmatic law of the king, to preserve public order.

182.label: The Brisk Method (R. Chaim Soloveitchik) and Academic Study
182.bio: A discussion of the Brisk method against academic-historical approaches to study: where the tension lies, and what can be gained without blurring boundaries.
182.core_concept: The tool is not the goal: the question is the learner's awareness, fear of Heaven and the purpose of study.

16.label: The Rambam Revolution, the Spanish Response and the Rema's Legacy
16.bio: An intellectual drama about the purpose of Torah study: the Rambam sets metaphysical apprehension as the summit, while the Sages of Spain stress the centrality of the Gemara and at times of Kabbalah. The Rema shapes a model in which the study of halakha and Talmud is itself the goal, and so lays the foundations of the yeshiva world. The chapter points to implications for the question of the authority of the Oral Torah.
16.core_concept: The debate over the purpose of the Torah: halakha as the goal versus philosophy or Kabbalah as the summit – and the shaping of the yeshiva world.

52.label: The Ritva — the kabbalist who defended the philosopher
52.bio: One of the great sages of Spain and author of fundamental novellae. In "Sefer HaZikaron" he presents a complex defence of the Rambam alongside loyalty to Kabbalah.
52.core_concept: Forty-nine faces: the Torah contains many opinions from the start; dispute is a way of revelation, not a fault.

50.label: Rabbi Abraham Abulafia
50.bio: A radical kabbalist who developed a path to prophecy through letter combinations and exercises, and met fierce opposition.
50.core_concept: Turning Kabbalah into a systematic path to mystical attainment – consciousness, language, breath and the active intellect.

340.label: Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu
340.bio: Rishon LeZion and Chief Rabbi of Israel. He combined halakhic ruling with the tradition of Kabbalah and the Ari.
340.core_concept: Unity of the revealed and the hidden within the world of halakha.

192.label: Abraham ibn Ezra
192.bio: A rationalist commentator and scientist who combined plain-sense interpretation with kabbalistic depth and scientific knowledge.
192.core_concept: Interpretation by the plain sense, clear language with hidden depth, a combination of astrology and science.

2.label: Shimon ben Shetach
2.bio: A courageous leader who worked for social justice and the rule of law. He stood up to King Yannai and saved the Oral Torah.
2.core_concept: Law and ethics together. Reforms as a way of preserving the Torah.

285.label: Rabbenu Manoach of Narbonne
285.bio: One of the important commentators on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah. In his "Sefer HaMenuchah" he sought to reconcile the Rambam's rulings with the Talmud, the Yerushalmi, the halakhic midrashim and the Ra'avad's critical glosses.
285.core_concept: Bringing the learner to "rest" by resolving contradictions and showing the roots of the Rambam's rulings in rabbinic sources.

294.label: Rabbi Aharon HaLevi
294.bio: A student of the Ramban and one of the pillars of the Catalan school, which combined Tosafist depth with Spanish clarity. In his work "Bedek HaBayit" he re-examined the Rashba's "Torat HaBayit".
294.core_concept: Loyalty to tradition is not only preservation but a fresh, responsible examination that keeps halakha alive and precise.

11.label: Rabbi Yehuda HeChasid (Ashkenazi Pietists)
11.bio: A leader of the Ashkenazi Pietists who placed purity of heart above sharpness of mind and joined ethics with prayer as a repair of the worlds; he also had influence through a controversial "Testament".
11.core_concept: Everyday holiness: self-sacrifice as an ongoing state of mind – self-control, truth and devotion.

325.label: The Chida (Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai)
325.bio: A halakhic authority, kabbalist and historian who wrote "Shem HaGedolim" and became a key figure in Jewish cultural memory.
325.core_concept: Combining manuscript research, ruling and Kabbalah.

336.label: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef
336.bio: One of the greatest halakhic authorities of the last generation and the spiritual leader of Sephardi Jewry. He restored the centrality of Sephardi ruling and founded a social and Torah revival movement.
336.core_concept: Restoring the crown to its former glory, and joining halakha with public responsibility.

449.label: Rabbi Israel Isserlein
449.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of Ashkenaz and a central shaper of the Ashkenazi tradition of ruling and custom.
449.core_concept: Halakha and custom together build a living culture.

457.label: Rabbi Yaakov Pollak
457.bio: One of those who moved the centre of Torah to Poland, and one of the developers of the yeshiva method of pilpul.
457.core_concept: Scholarly sharpness as a tool for revealing the depth of the Torah.

335.label: The Lubavitcher Rebbe
335.bio: The seventh leader of Chabad Hasidism, who built a worldwide network of emissaries and turned responsibility for every Jew into a universal vision.
335.core_concept: Making the world "a dwelling place in the lower realms" through mission and action.

266.label: Rabbenu Yehuda ben Barzilai of Barcelona
266.bio: One of the great sages of Spain at the start of the age of the Rishonim, who sought to fortify the tradition of the Geonim through broad, detailed codes. He wrote comprehensive halakhic works and also included theological inquiry.
266.core_concept: Preserving the teaching of the Geonim through a broad halakhic encyclopedia, while laying foundations for early Jewish rationalism.

287.label: Rabbi Nathan ben Meir of Trinquetaille
287.bio: One of the great sages of Provence, who joined the dialectic of the Tosafists, Provençal system and the authority of the Rif and the Ra'avad. He deeply influenced the Ramban and the tradition of ruling.
287.core_concept: Creating a scholarly method that links France, Provence and Spain, and serves as a foundation for the Ramban's way.

341.label: Rabbi Shmuel Salant
341.bio: The Ashkenazi rabbi of Jerusalem for decades and one of the shapers of the city's Jewish community.
341.core_concept: Building Jerusalem through institutions, public responsibility and balanced rulings.

17.label: Rabbi Yosef Albo
17.bio: A student of Crescas and a representative at the Disputation of Tortosa. He distilled the foundations of faith into three principles and built a structure of roots and branches.
17.core_concept: Theological flexibility: a distinction between error and heresy; faith as moral steadfastness; an emphasis on free will against determinism.

23.label: Menachem ben Saruq — the Hebrew language revolution
23.bio: Menachem ben Saruq as a pioneer of Hebrew grammar: the "Machberet", the shaping of the system of roots and patterns, and the debate with Dunash ben Labrat.
23.core_concept: Clarifying Hebrew as a tool of identity and a basis for understanding Scripture and building Jewish culture in Spain.

24.label: Hasdai ibn Shaprut
24.bio: A brilliant Jew who rose to the top of the Muslim court in Córdoba. He built a spiritual future for Spanish Jewry.
24.core_concept: Combining Jewish identity with political influence; leadership from within the wider world.

43.label: Rabbi Yitzchak of Vienna (Or Zarua)
43.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of Ashkenaz, who wrote a Talmudic and halakhic encyclopedia with a revolutionary combination of the Bavli and the Yerushalmi.
43.core_concept: Textual depth, boldness in ruling, and a combination of tradition and innovation, of community and individual.

53.label: The Mordechai (Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel)
53.bio: A central halakhic authority who gathered a whole world of Ashkenazi halakha just before it was destroyed. His book preserved the Tosafist tradition and influenced the Rema.
53.core_concept: Combining study with custom, grammar with poetry, depth with order, in a time of existential crisis.

51.label: Rabbi Menachem HaMeiri
51.bio: A brilliant thinker from Provence, author of "Beit HaBechirah". He combined rational philosophy with orderly scholarship and advocated a universal ethical approach to halakha.
51.core_concept: A distinction between idolaters and ethical nations, system in halakha, and sensitivity to biblical interpretation.

151.label: Emmanuel Levinas
151.bio: A Jewish philosopher who placed responsibility for the other before understanding. He changed the foundations of modern ethical thought.
151.core_concept: The other comes before knowledge. Responsibility comes before the concept.

267.label: The Kuzari
267.bio: One of the foundational works of Jewish thought, written by Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi in Judeo-Arabic. It offers an original defence of Judaism through history, national revelation and the bond between people, commandments and Land.
267.core_concept: Grounding Jewish faith in national historical memory and public revelation, not only in abstract philosophical proof.

279.label: The Ritzba
279.bio: One of the central figures of the generation after Rabbenu Tam in the world of the Tosafot. He combined scholarly independence and wide use of the Yerushalmi with a reputation as a man of visions and of the secrets of creation.
279.core_concept: A rare union of Talmudic dialectical sharpness and mystical depth, as a bridge between Ashkenaz, Spain and the worlds of mystery.

284.label: Rabbi Yehuda ben Berachia
284.bio: A sage of Provence who wrote a broad commentary on the Rif's Halakhot. His method combined plain sense, criticism of the Rif, the tradition of the Geonim and comparison with the Rambam's rulings.
284.core_concept: Making Provence a living bridge between the tradition of the Geonim, the Rif, the Rambam and the Tosafists.

286.label: Rabbi Reuven ben Chaim of Narbonne
286.bio: A Provençal sage and philosopher who worked at the crossroads of the Tosafists, the Rambam and the halakhic tradition of the Ra'avad. His "Sefer HaTamid" combined halakha, liturgy and philosophy.
286.core_concept: Turning the order of prayer and the Jewish day into a space of study that joins halakha, the interpretation of prayer and Maimonidean thought.

469.label: Rabbi Crescas Vidal
469.bio: A student of the Rashba and the Ra'ah, known as a central mediator in the controversy over philosophy in Spanish Jewry.
469.core_concept: A balance between openness of thought and loyalty to tradition.

467.label: Rabbi Israel Sarug
467.bio: One of those who spread the Kabbalah of the Ari in Europe and developed a central stream of Lurianic Kabbalah.
467.core_concept: Spreading wisdom is part of the process of redemption.

67.label: Don Isaac Abravanel — statesman, philosopher, exegete
67.bio: A statesman and central Bible commentator; he wrote comprehensive commentaries and philosophical-messianic books out of the experience of expulsion and wandering.
67.core_concept: A historical-theological reading of Scripture and history as a way of shaping identity and hope in exile.

198.label: Dunash ben Labrat
198.bio: The poet and linguist who revolutionised Hebrew poetry and brought Arabic metre into it.
198.core_concept: Creating a self-aware, artistic Hebrew poetry.

38.label: The Sages of Provence — Narbonne and early mysticism
38.bio: Provence is portrayed as a meeting ground between systematic Spanish halakha and Ashkenazi-French dialectic, and as a political and Torah centre around Narbonne and its tradition of nesi'im. Out of that tension early Kabbalah was born, in synthesis with the Ashkenazi Pietists. The chapter shows how a small regional centre changed the spiritual map of the Middle Ages and prepared the ground for later developments.
38.core_concept: The meeting of traditions as an engine of creativity: a Spanish–Ashkenazi synthesis that gives birth to a new halakhic and mystical centre.

42.label: Rabbi Isaac the Blind (Sagi Nahor)
42.bio: Called "the father of Kabbalah", the son of the Ra'avad of Posquières, he was active in Provence at the end of the 12th century and the start of the 13th. Blind from birth, he developed an abstract thought on the Ein Sof and the sefirot, and turned the teaching of mystery from an oral tradition into an ordered system that, through his students from Girona, influenced great figures of the generation such as the Ramban.
42.core_concept: Kabbalah as the inner layer of the Torah and prayer: thought on the Ein Sof and the sefirot that grew at the heart of the Torah establishment, not at its margins.

343.label: Rabbi David Abudarham
343.bio: Author of a fundamental commentary on the prayers and blessings that greatly influenced the rulings of the Shulchan Arukh.
343.core_concept: Joining the meaning of prayer, halakha and custom.

264.label: Mahari Bruna
264.bio: One of the central halakhic authorities of 15th-century Ashkenaz, who lived through expulsions, imprisonments and a blood libel. The responsa of Mahari Bruna became a foundational source in the glosses of the Rema.
264.core_concept: Preserving the continuity of Ashkenazi halakha through realistic, responsible rulings in a time of persecution and communal crisis.

64.label: Mahari Mintz
64.bio: A rabbi in Renaissance Italy who combined halakhic tradition with a complex cultural reality.
64.core_concept: Combining loyalty to halakha with responsible cultural openness.

69.label: The Radbaz (1479–1573)
69.bio: The Radbaz as a supreme halakhic authority and leader: wanderings from Spain to Egypt and the Land of Israel, practical rulings on difficult questions, and enormous influence through the Responsa of the Radbaz.
69.core_concept: Responsible halakhic flexibility: loyalty to tradition alongside answers to the new reality of expulsion and economy.

70.label: The Maharshal (Rabbi Shlomo Luria)
70.bio: A halakhic authority and revolutionary in study who opposed "pilpul" and advocated precision and a return to the sources. He stood against the Rema in a dispute of ideas.
70.core_concept: Halakhic integrity and original criticism, meticulous precision and a return to the Talmudic sources.

74.label: Rabbi Elazar Azikri
74.bio: A kabbalist and member of the Safed circles, he founded a fellowship for repentance and devotion and wrote "Sefer Charedim"; his poem "Yedid Nefesh" became a prayer of the heart for generations.
74.core_concept: Mapping the personal service of God: every limb becomes a vessel of holiness – "within my heart I will build a sanctuary".

85.label: Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes — Mishneh LaMelech
85.bio: R. Yehuda Rosanes, author of the "Mishneh LaMelech": building logical arguments on the Rambam, clarifying the views of the Rishonim, and a deep influence on the way of study.
85.core_concept: Halakha as a systematic wisdom: not only practical ruling but a methodology that clarifies principles and structures.

113.label: Rabbi Israel Salanter
113.bio: Founder of the Mussar movement, he set inner work at the heart of Torah life and saw character traits as the foundation of repentance.
113.core_concept: A psychological distinction between intellect and emotion – only through ethics and inner work does a person change.

347.label: Solomon Munk
347.bio: An orientalist and scholar of Judaism who returned ibn Gabirol to the history of philosophy and edited the Guide of the Perplexed from the Arabic original.
347.core_concept: Combining scholarly research with loyalty to tradition.

146.label: Chacham Menachem Menashe
146.bio: A hidden tzaddik who worked as a simple tinsmith by day and a kabbalist by night. He wrote the book "Ahavat Chaim" and influenced many communities with devotion and humility.
146.core_concept: Holiness out of concealment and humility; kindness as a cosmic spiritual engine; joining halakha with simple life.

154.label: Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi
154.bio: A kabbalist and leader who founded the Nahar Shalom yeshiva to preserve the tradition of kavanot after the destruction of Beit El; he lived simply and radiated love of Israel and rare humility.
154.core_concept: The service of God as humility and service: lofty kavanot alongside complete accessibility to every person.

148.label: Mr. Shoshani
148.bio: An enigmatic figure and an elusive genius. He took things apart and pushed towards independent thinking without leaving an ordered system.
148.core_concept: The question as an opening to truth. There is no final interpretation of the Torah.

166.label: Rabbi Yehuda Léon Askénazi (Manitou)
166.bio: A thinker and kabbalist who joined the North African tradition, French intellectual discourse and the Torah of the Land of Israel; he formulated a doctrine of identities and set out a new language of revival.
166.core_concept: The "Hebrew" identity as a stage of national consciousness that unites sacred and secular, family and people, ethics and history.

175.label: Chacham Yeshua Ben-Shushan — the kabbalist commando commander
175.bio: A fighter and commander in elite reconnaissance units alongside a life of Kabbalah and prayer. A figure who joins heroism, national responsibility and an awareness of redemption.
175.core_concept: A rare combination of worlds: mystical service of God alongside a fighting ethos and public mission.

351.label: Rabbi Nathan of Rome
351.bio: Author of the first comprehensive Talmudic dictionary, "Sefer HeArukh", which preserved the legacy of the Geonim and made the language of the Talmud accessible.
351.core_concept: Linguistic precision as the key to understanding the Torah.

190.label: Abraham bar Chiya
190.bio: The first Jew to write science in Hebrew; he influenced the translation of Eastern learning into Europe.
190.core_concept: Combining Torah, science and philosophy; translating general wisdom into Hebrew.

280.label: Rabbi Elazar of Worms (the Rokeach)
280.bio: One of the great sages of Ashkenaz, a halakhic authority and kabbalist whose teaching grew out of a terrible personal tragedy. In the "Sefer HaRokeach" he combined halakha, custom, ethics and mystery.
280.core_concept: Seeing prayer and the commandments as precise spiritual structures of letters and meanings, joining strict halakha with mystical experience.

275.label: Ri HaZaken of Dampierre
275.bio: One of the great Tosafists and a central leader after Rabbenu Tam. In his yeshiva in Dampierre he created a model of collective study in which the whole Talmud is seen as one harmonious system.
275.core_concept: Building a collective, comparative method of study that reconciles contradictions between sugyot and shapes the Talmud as one living body.

283.label: Rabbi Meshulam of Béziers
283.bio: One of the great sages of Provence and author of "Sefer HaHashlamah", who sought to complete and update the Rif. He defended the Rambam but fought early kabbalistic works that seemed to him to endanger the purity of faith.
283.core_concept: Uniting deep scholarship, loyalty to tradition and intellectual courage in the struggle for the purity of faith and for the Provençal way of halakha.

415.label: Rabbi Shem Tov ibn Gaon
415.bio: A halakhic authority, kabbalist and scholar of the Masorah who joined the Rambam's system, Kabbalah and the art of sacred writing.
415.core_concept: Halakha and Kabbalah are different faces of the same truth.

424.label: Rabbi Vidal of Tolosa
424.bio: The Rambam's central commentator, who uncovered the sources and method of the Mishneh Torah.
424.core_concept: Understanding the depth behind halakhic rulings.

433.label: Rabbi Yosef Chaviva
433.bio: Author of the "Nimukei Yosef", a central summariser of the teaching of the later sages of Spain who made it accessible.
433.core_concept: Preserving the continuity of Torah through clarity and order.

444.label: The Maharil
444.bio: The father of the customs of Ashkenaz and one of the shapers of the halakhic and liturgical identity of Ashkenazi Jewry.
444.core_concept: Custom is the living memory of the generations.

452.label: Rabbi Yaakov Landau
452.bio: Author of "Sefer HaAgur" and one of the pioneers of carrying the halakhic tradition into the age of print.
452.core_concept: Keeping tradition through order, precision and accessibility.

458.label: Rabbi Shalom Shachna of Lublin
458.bio: A central head of a yeshiva in Poland and teacher of the Rema, one of the shapers of the Polish yeshiva world.
458.core_concept: The Torah should remain a living process of study and judgement.

464.label: Rabbi Yehoshua ibn Shu'eib
464.bio: A student of the Rashba and one of the great preachers of Spain, who made deep ideas accessible to the wider public.
464.core_concept: Joining halakha, faith and practical life.

196.label: Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook
196.bio: Successor of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook and leader of the generation of revival of religious Zionism.
196.core_concept: Joining the State of Israel, Torah study and redemption.

8.label: Rabbah bar bar Chana
8.bio: His fantastic legends are a secret code of exile and redemption, parables about the depths of history and faith.
8.core_concept: Aggadah as a theological tool. Where reason stops, imagination begins to teach.

81.label: Isaac Nunes Belmonte (1601–1652)
81.bio: Isaac Nunes Belmonte: a former converso in the Dutch world, a struggle of identity and a search for a path through philosophy and medicine.
81.core_concept: Identity as a conscious choice: the tension between tradition, freedom and modernity shows especially in the stories of the conversos.

12.label: Rabbenu Bachya ben Asher
12.bio: An innovative commentator who made Kabbalah, ethics and midrash accessible to all Israel in clear language, and who developed the PaRDeS approach.
12.core_concept: Combining four layers in one systematic commentary – plain sense, allusion, homily and mystery at the heart of interpretation.

57.label: Rabbi Hasdai Crescas
57.bio: Leader of Aragonese Jewry in the riots of 1391 and a revolutionary philosopher. He set love at the centre and broke Aristotelian foundations.
57.core_concept: A loving God and continuous creation; freedom and choice against determinism; ideas on space and infinity that anticipated modern science.

459.label: The Maharik (Rabbi Yosef Colon)
459.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities who gave communal custom a central place in ruling.
459.core_concept: Custom is part of the living Torah of the people of Israel.

18.label: Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura
18.bio: He came to the Land of Israel after a gruelling journey and led the impoverished Jerusalem community under the Mamluks. He founded charitable institutions and revived the Jewish settlement.
18.core_concept: Holiness joined with action: a clear, comprehensive commentary on the Mishnah alongside a revolution in communal leadership that prepared the absorption of the exiles from Spain.

19.label: Rabbi Yosef Chayun
19.bio: Leader of the Lisbon community and teacher of Abravanel. He offered a solution to the question of the words Moses spoke "of his own accord", and the principle that the Bible never says the same thing twice.
19.core_concept: Moses composed the speeches, but God dictated them to him word for word when the Torah was written; every word in Scripture is unique and there are no mere "synonyms".

27.label: Rav Shmuel ben Chofni Gaon
27.bio: One of the great Geonim of Babylonia. He wrote dozens of systematic halakhic books and stressed that aggadah is conceptual guidance but no basis for ruling.
27.core_concept: Purifying the bounds of decision: halakha as binding; filtering out magical notions and resting faith on common sense and loyalty to tradition.

35.label: Rabbenu Chananel ben Chushiel
35.bio: The greatest halakhic authority of Kairouan and the first to write a systematic commentary on the Babylonian Talmud. He summed up the sugyot clearly and prepared the ground for the Rif and the Rambam.
35.core_concept: Mapping the sea of sugyot into a halakhic path: concision, clarifying the text, and the systematic use of the Yerushalmi for decision.

46.label: Rabbi Zerachia HaLevi (Baal HaMaor)
46.bio: Author of "Sefer HaMaor", who opened an independent discussion of the Rif's sugyot and set a model of integrity in Torah and textual criticism; he stirred a controversy with the Ra'avad and won the recognition of the Ramban.
46.core_concept: The pursuit of truth that gives birth to critical study loyal to tradition – not blind acceptance.

49.label: The Ra'avia (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yoel HaLevi)
49.bio: A man who brought a dialectical approach to the Ashkenazi tradition, combined sharpness with keeping custom, and wrote "Avi HaEzri".
49.core_concept: The courage to rule from an understanding of custom, combining intellectual sharpness with sensitivity to reality.

54.label: Rabbi Yechiel of Paris
54.bio: He stood at the Paris trial (1240) against the charges brought against the Talmud. Despite his arguments, 24 cartloads of manuscripts were burned; he is regarded as a symbol of public courage.
54.core_concept: An interpretive, systematic defence of rabbinic literature at a historic moment; Torah influence through students and a great yeshiva in Paris.

56.label: The Rivash (Rabbi Yitzchak bar Sheshet)
56.bio: Student of the Ran and supreme halakhic authority. He fled to Algiers as an elderly refugee and led thousands of refugees; his responsa are a "human diary" of a community's rebuilding.
56.core_concept: Rulings with compassion: the status of forced converts, women's rights, the power of the community; keeping the boundaries of faith against philosophy as a "danger".

92.label: Rabbi Avraham Gershon of Kitov (1701–1761)
92.bio: R. Avraham Gershon of Kitov, brother-in-law of the Baal Shem Tov: his move to the Land of Israel, a spiritual mission, and letters that shed light on the beginnings of Hasidism.
92.core_concept: The Land of Israel as a space of repair: Hasidism seeks to bring holiness down into reality and place.

76.label: Rabbi Yoel Sirkis (the Bach)
76.bio: Author of the "Bayit Chadash", a bold and profound halakhic authority who insisted on learning halakha from the sources. He combined homily, scholarship and custom, and led the Council of Four Lands.
76.core_concept: He opposed superficial ruling from the Shulchan Arukh; he demanded depth, context and analysis of the Rishonim in every ruling. He ruled to permit new grain in a time of hardship.

87.label: Rabbi Ephraim Navon (1677–1735) — Machaneh Ephraim
87.bio: Rabbi Ephraim Navon, author of the "Machaneh Ephraim": ordering the principles of the laws of acquisition and property, clarifying the views of the Rishonim, and setting out a clear system of rules.
87.core_concept: Precision at the root of the sugya: strong rulings are built from understanding the structure of the law, not merely from piling up sources.

202.label: Rabbi Akiva Eger
202.bio: The humble genius who shaped modern yeshiva scholarship.
202.core_concept: Sharp questions and analytical thinking as an educational and Talmudic tool.

203.label: Rabbi Eliyahu Guttmacher
203.bio: A kabbalist and forerunner of religious Zionism who saw settlement of the Land as the beginning of redemption.
203.core_concept: Redemption begins with action – settlement, agriculture and the commandments that depend on the Land.

111.label: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Chajes (Maharatz Chajes)
111.bio: A great Torah scholar in Galicia who tried to bridge careful research and absolute loyalty to the Oral Torah, and built a language of intellectual defence of tradition.
111.core_concept: A faithful bridge: open-mindedness that serves faith – and does not replace it.

130.label: The Alter of Novardok — the Mussar revolution
130.bio: A student of R. Israel Salanter and founder of the "Beit Yosef" network of yeshivot. He developed a radical educational method of improving character and total reliance on God.
130.core_concept: Mussar exercises as a laboratory of the soul: exposing hidden motives and building practical courage of faith.

338.label: Rabbi Abdallah Somekh
338.bio: The greatest sage of Babylonia in the 19th century and teacher of the Ben Ish Chai. He rebuilt the centre of Torah in Baghdad.
338.core_concept: Responsible ruling connected to reality and to the needs of the community.

126.label: The Ben Ish Chai (Rabbi Yosef Chaim of Baghdad)
126.bio: A great halakhic authority, kabbalist and renowned preacher of the Sephardi world in Baghdad, who wrote the "Ben Ish Chai" – a combination of halakha, aggadah and Kabbalah.
126.core_concept: Joining Kabbalah and halakha; popular writing accessible to the wider public with an ethical touch.

128.label: Rabbi Meir Simcha of Dvinsk
128.bio: Author of "Or Same'ach" and "Meshech Chochmah". A bridge between reason and faith, and between exile and revival; a sharp analysis of Jewish history and holiness.
128.core_concept: Exile as a mechanism of identity; holiness lies not in matter but in God's will; Zionism and redemption by natural means (Balfour, San Remo).

137.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Alfiya
137.bio: A Jerusalem kabbalist who worked in mighty quiet. He instituted the speech fast as a deep spiritual repair for our time.
137.core_concept: The power of silence; repairing the world through simplicity and devotion; repairing speech in an unbridled generation.

169.label: Elie Wiesel
169.bio: A Holocaust survivor and great writer. He joined brokenness to faith and memory to a moral call.
169.core_concept: Memory as responsibility. Faith as struggle. Restlessness as a commandment.

150.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri
150.bio: The elder of the kabbalists, who lived in immense humility and had a deep influence on the tradition of mystery, practical Kabbalah and public spirituality.
150.core_concept: Kabbalah as life, not only theory. Leadership through silence and responsibility.

334.label: Rabbi Yosef Qafih
334.bio: A judge, scholar and translator who restored the writings of the Rambam and the Rishonim of Spain to their precise text from Yemenite manuscripts.
334.core_concept: Combining loyalty to tradition with scholarly research and textual precision.

174.label: Rabbi Refael Moshe Luria
174.bio: A student of Slonim who moved from heading a yeshiva to the depths of mystery after a medical crisis; he developed original ideas on the contraction of holiness, the holiness of the Land and the essence of sacrifice.
174.core_concept: "The contraction of holiness" as a historical and spiritual pattern: concentrating light in one place in order to shine from it with force.

478.label: Rabbi Israel Abuhatzeira (the Baba Sali)
478.bio: A kabbalist and tzaddik of the Abuhatzeira family, grandson of the "Abir Yaakov". He came from Morocco and settled in Netivot, which became a centre of pilgrimage. He was known for his asceticism, his prayers and his blessings.
478.core_concept: Holiness and asceticism as a tool of public leadership – personal devotion that radiates onto a whole people.

189.label: Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher (the Tur)
189.bio: The Ba'al HaTurim, author of the "Arba'ah Turim", who arranged halakha into an organising structure of four main fields.
189.core_concept: Dividing halakha into four "rows"; a systematic approach that orders the disputes rather than erasing them.

271.label: The Re'em of Metz
271.bio: One of the great Rishonim of France and Ashkenaz, a student of Rabbenu Tam and the Rashbam. In his "Sefer Yere'im" he presented the commandments not only as a system of laws but as a way of shaping the person.
271.core_concept: Arranging the commandments as a comprehensive spiritual and ethical structure in which halakha is meant to shape the soul, not only to decide the law.

393.label: Rabbi Meir ben Shimon HaMe'ili
393.bio: A halakhic authority and thinker who worked in Narbonne and defended the principle of God's unity and the legacy of the Rambam.
393.core_concept: Loyalty to tradition alongside an intellectual struggle for faith.

390.label: Rabbenu Shmuel HaSardi
390.bio: One of the great sages of Spain and author of "Sefer HaTerumot", one of the cornerstones of Jewish law.
390.core_concept: Turning halakha into a practical, systematic legal system.

288.label: Rabbenu Perachia ben Nissim
288.bio: One of the prominent sages of Egypt in the generation after the Rambam, who wrote commentaries on the Rif's Halakhot and stood at the forefront of defending the Rambam's teaching against its opponents.
288.core_concept: Preserving the Rambam's legacy and continuing his Talmudic method, with public responsibility for the Maimonidean tradition.

386.label: Rabbi Chananel ben Shmuel
386.bio: Head of the judges in Fustat and one of the leaders of Egyptian Jewry after the Rambam.
386.core_concept: Combining halakha, public leadership and inner service of God.

300.label: Rabbi Simcha of Speyer
300.bio: A halakhic authority and leader who rebuilt Ashkenazi Jewry after the Crusades. He combined halakha with social building and stood behind central communal ordinances.
300.core_concept: Halakha as a tool for building community and not only for private rulings.

301.label: The Riaz (Rabbi Isaiah di Trani the Younger)

407.label: Rabbi Meir HaKohen of Rothenburg
407.bio: A student of the Maharam of Rothenburg and author of the "Hagahot Maimoniyot", a bridge between the Rambam and the tradition of Ashkenaz.
407.core_concept: Preserving custom and tradition within the halakhic code.

308.label: The Rid (Rabbi Isaiah di Trani the Elder)
308.bio: He created a new method of study that focuses on understanding each sugya on its own terms, even at the cost of leaving contradictions open.
308.core_concept: "A dwarf on the shoulders of a giant" – the creative continuity of tradition.

309.label: Rabbi Avigdor Katz of Vienna
309.bio: A leader who joined the traditions of Italy, Ashkenaz and France and made Vienna a significant centre of Torah.
309.core_concept: Creating a synthesis of different methods of study into one tradition.

310.label: Rabbi Menachem ben Zerach
310.bio: A halakhic authority who wrote "Tzedah LaDerech" – a clear, accessible halakhic guide for busy people living under cultural pressure.
310.core_concept: Halakha with reasons – combining clarity with conceptual understanding.

311.label: Rabbi Yehuda ben HaRosh
311.bio: Leader of Spanish Jewry after the Rosh, who combined the methods of Ashkenaz and Spain and built a broad halakhic authority.
311.core_concept: A synthesis of Ashkenazi study and Spanish ruling.

314.label: Rabbi Yitzchak of Düren
314.bio: Author of "Sha'arei Dura" – a foundational book on the laws of the forbidden and the permitted that shaped Jewish home and kitchen life for generations.
314.core_concept: Bringing halakha from the yeshiva into the home.

sup-45.label: Rashi (Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac)
sup-45.bio: The greatest of medieval commentators, his interpretations on the Torah and Talmud became the foundation of Jewish biblical exegesis. His commentary towers over all others, and his school of thought shaped Jewish learning.

sup-46.label: Hillel the Elder
sup-46.bio: A founding sage of the Tannaim and pioneer of broad interpretive methods (the thirteen rules). His principle 'Love peace in the world' became the cornerstone of his entire teaching.

sup-47.label: Shammai
sup-47.bio: Hillel's great debate partner, representing the stricter interpretation of law. His school preserved the severity and strictness of halakha, though Hillel's rulings prevailed in practice.

sup-48.label: Rabbi Judah the Prince (Rebbi)
sup-48.bio: End of the Tannaim era; compiler of the Mishnah, the foundational text of the Oral Torah. His editing of the teachings became the basis for all subsequent Jewish law.

sup-49.label: The Baal Shem Tov (Besht)
sup-49.bio: Founder of Hasidic Judaism, he elevated the common folk to a path of faith through simple-hearted devotion and joy. 'The Divine Presence dwells in all things.'

sup-50.label: The Vilna Gaon (Elijah ben Solomon)
sup-50.bio: A supreme Torah genius of unparalleled breadth. Opposed to Hasidism, he established Lithuanian yeshiva learning as the counterweight, emphasizing deep Talmudic study with Kabbalah and prayer.

sup-51.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Luria (The ARI)
sup-51.bio: Renewed Kabbalah through doctrines of tzimtzum, broken vessels, and tikkun. His teachings became the foundation of all subsequent mystical Judaism and profoundly influenced Hasidic thought.

sup-52.label: Isaac ibn Gikatilla
sup-52.bio: Early Spanish Kabbalist, author of 'Sha'are Orah' (Gates of Light), who synthesized Kabbalistic thought with Neoplatonic philosophy and Sufi influences.

sup-53.label: Ramchal (Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto)
sup-53.bio: Poet, philosopher, and kabbalist; author of the 'Path of the Just,' one of the greatest ethical works in Jewish tradition. His systematic approach to spirituality influenced all following generations.

sup-54.label: Solomon ibn Gabirol
sup-54.bio: Hebrew poet and Jewish-Islamic philosopher of Spain's Golden Age. His liturgical poetry, especially 'Royal Crown,' remains central to Jewish prayer, and his philosophical work 'Fountain of Life' shaped medieval thought.

sup-55.label: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin
sup-55.bio: Student of the Vilna Gaon and founder of the Volozhin Yeshiva, which became the model for all subsequent Ashkenazi yeshiva education. His work 'Soul of Life' presents the philosophical foundations of Lithuanian yeshiva study.

sup-56.label: Rabbi Yosel of Rosheim
sup-56.bio: Defender of Ashkenazi Jewry, advocate for peaceful relations between Jews and Christians in medieval Germany. His leadership during the Reformation era was crucial for Jewish survival.

sup-57.label: David al-Roi
sup-57.bio: A messianic pretender of medieval Baghdad whose movement, though short-lived, influenced subsequent messianic movements and kabbalistic thought about redemption.

sup-58.label: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai
sup-58.bio: Founding leader of the Yavneh Academy after the Temple's destruction. He secured the continuity of Judaism by obtaining Roman permission to establish a center of Jewish learning, saving the tradition during its darkest hour.

sup-59.label: Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef (continued influence)
sup-59.bio: Greatest of the later Tannaim, known for his expansive interpretive methods and role as a bridge between different halakhic schools. He died a martyr for Jewish faith.

sup-60.label: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sup-60.bio: Tanna sage famed for both halakhic rulings and mystical teachings. Tradition associates him with the authorship of the Zohar, the central text of Jewish Kabbalah, though scholars debate its dating.

sup-61.label: Rabbi Eliezer ben Dordia
sup-61.bio: Tanna known for his comprehensive knowledge of Torah and his powerful teshuva (repentance). His story in the Talmud is one of the most moving narratives about spiritual transformation.

sup-62.label: Rabbi Menachem ben Sapir
sup-62.bio: Amora of northern Israel, student of Rabbi Yochanan, active in transmitting halakhic rulings and Talmudic discussions.

sup-63.label: Rabbi Avraham Riba
sup-63.bio: Rabbi of Lvov (Poland), major halakhic authority whose rulings influenced Polish and Ukrainian Jewry. His innovations in halakhic reasoning were widely discussed.

sup-64.label: The Maharal of Prague
sup-64.bio: Preeminent ethical and mystical thinker who synthesized philosophy and Kabbalah. The Golem legends surrounding him became part of Jewish folklore worldwide.

sup-65.label: Menasseh ben Israel
sup-65.bio: Diplomat and scholar who negotiated the readmission of Jews to England after 300 years of exile. His 'Hope of Israel' argued for messianic restoration tied to the Jewish return to England.

sup-66.label: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer
sup-66.bio: Pioneer of religious Zionism, argued that settlement of Eretz Israel is a religious obligation. His 'Seeking Zion' proposed practical settlement as a path to redemption.

sup-67.label: Rabbi Reuven Margaliot
sup-67.bio: Modern Kabbalist and scholar of Midrash, discoverer of unknown Talmudic texts in the Cairo Genizah. His works preserved and analyzed vast amounts of Jewish mystical and halakhic literature.

sup-68.label: Rabbi Yaakov Kaniel
sup-68.bio: Great Lithuanian yeshiva master of the mid-20th century, known for his profound Talmudic insights and ethical teachings.

sup-69.label: Rabbi Yosef Sholom Elyashiv
sup-69.bio: Foremost halakhic authority of modern Jerusalem. For decades he was consulted on complex legal questions from communities worldwide. His rulings shaped modern Jewish practice.

sup-70.label: Rabbi Yitzhak Staler
sup-70.bio: Bridge figure between Lithuanian rationalism and Hasidic emotion. Student of both Vilna Gaon's disciples and Hasidic masters, he represented a unified approach to Jewish spirituality.

sup-71.label: Rabbi Natan Tzvi Finkel
sup-71.bio: Founder of the Mir Yeshiva. Pioneer of the ethical mussar movement, he elevated practical morality as the foundation of Torah study and transformed yeshiva education.

sup-72.label: Rabbi Avraham Kuba
sup-72.bio: Community leader of mid-20th century Bnei Brak, founder of Sephardic institutions. Known for his humility and dedication to preserving Sephardic tradition.

sup-73.label: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson (The Rebbe)
sup-73.bio: Seventh Rebbe of Chabad, led the worldwide Chabad movement for over 40 years. His teachings blend Hasidic thought with modern education and social action.

sup-74.label: Rabbi Yaakov Kaminetzki
sup-74.bio: Great Lithuanian yeshiva leader known for his incisive halakhic rulings and philosophical approach to Jewish law. His simplicity in approach belied profound depth.

sup-75.label: Rabbi Moshe Feinstein
sup-75.bio: Supreme halakhic authority of the 20th century. His 'Iggerot Moshe' (Letters of Moshe) addressed modern halakhic questions from thousands of questioners worldwide with clarity and compassion.

sup-76.label: Rabbi Yosef Boer
sup-76.bio: Great builder of Torah institutions in Israel, leader of Yeshiva Chevron. Authority on halakha of Eretz Israel and its sanctity.

sup-77.label: Rabbi Shmuel Kamenetsky
sup-77.bio: Dean of Philadelphia Yeshiva, leading figure in ethical education. Known for his integration of moral teaching with Talmudic scholarship.

sup-78.label: Rabbi Yaakov Emden
sup-78.bio: Son of the Chacham Tzvi, halakhic authority and kabbalist. His responsa addressed major Jewish theological questions of the 18th century and his works on prayer remain influential.

sup-79.label: Rabbi Avraham Levi Horowitz
sup-79.bio: Author of 'Gedulat Avraham,' he bridged Hasidic fervor with Lithuanian rationalism. Represented the synthesis of these two traditions that characterized certain yeshiva leaders.

sup-80.label: Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky
sup-80.bio: Preeminent Talmudic scholar of the late 20th century, known for his encyclopedic knowledge and rapid halachic rulings. His 'Piskei Teshuvot' addressed contemporary halakhic dilemmas.

sup-81.label: Rabbi Salach bar Yaakov
sup-81.bio: Babylonian Gaon whose teachings were preserved by his many students. Influential in establishing principles of Talmudic interpretation.

sup-82.label: Saadia Gaon
sup-82.bio: Supreme Gaon of Babylonia, founder of medieval Jewish philosophy. His 'Book of Beliefs and Opinions' created a systematic Jewish theology synthesizing Torah with reason.

sup-83.label: Natan ha-Bavi
sup-83.bio: Tanna of the early second century, transmitter of halakhic traditions and known for his careful transmission of the teachings.

sup-84.label: Rav (Abba Arika)
sup-84.bio: Founder of Sura Academy in Babylonia, he established the institution that would become the center of Jewish learning for centuries. His rulings formed the basis of Talmudic discussions.

sup-85.label: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sup-85.bio: Student of Rabbi Yochanan, collector of Tannaic traditions. His organized compilations of teachings ('Chiyya's Baraita') preserved much of the Oral Torah.

sup-86.label: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
sup-86.bio: Amoraic sage known for his numerous aggadic teachings and interpretations. His sermons preserved important homiletic traditions.

sup-87.label: Rabbi Yose ben Chanina
sup-87.bio: Third-generation Amora of Palestine, student of Rabbi Yochanan. Known for his generous interpretations in aggadah and halakhic creativity.

sup-88.label: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
sup-88.bio: Major amoraic authority in Palestine who served as successor to Rabbi Yochanan. His extensive teachings are woven throughout the Talmud and Midrashim.

sup-89.label: Rabbi Zusha of Annipoli
sup-89.bio: Brother of the Rebbe of Lizhensk, exemplar of Hasidic devotion. Known for his humble spirituality and deep integration of Hasidic teachings into daily life. His disciples transmitted his teachings with reverence.

521.label: Aaron the High Priest
521.bio: The first High Priest, Moses' brother and spokesman. 'Loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah.'
521.core_concept: "Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them closer to the Torah" – drawing people near through love and personal care, not through rebuke and fear.

505.label: Hillel the Elder
505.bio: Nasi of Israel and head of Beit Hillel. Came up from Babylonia; placed humility and love at the center: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow — that is the whole Torah.'
505.core_concept: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow" – a founding moral principle, alongside humility and sensitivity to reality as the foundation of halakhic ruling in the House of Hillel.

504.label: Shammai the Elder
504.bio: Head of the court and of Beit Shammai, Hillel's disputant. Ruled strictly out of an ideal of perfection, and taught: 'Say little and do much.'
504.core_concept: Setting the ideal of perfection as the focus of halakha – a principled difference from the House of Hillel, who focused on existing reality and not only on the potential of aspiration.

anc-4.label: Moses (Moshe Rabbenu)
anc-4.bio: Master of the prophets and receiver of the Torah at Sinai. Led Israel out of Egypt, received the Tablets, and transmitted the Torah to all Israel — head of the chain of transmission.

anc-2.label: Isaac the Patriarch
anc-2.bio: Second of the Patriarchs. Bound upon the altar on Mount Moriah; re-dug his father's wells, continuing the path in the Land.

anc-8.label: King David
anc-8.bio: Founder of the Davidic dynasty and author of the Book of Psalms. Conquered Jerusalem and brought up the Ark — 'the sweet singer of Israel'.

anc-7.label: Samuel the Prophet
anc-7.bio: Last of the judges and the greatest prophet after Moses. Established the monarchy in Israel and anointed Saul and David.

anc-1.label: Abraham the Patriarch
anc-1.bio: Father of the nation. Left Ur of the Chaldees at the call of 'Lech Lecha', spread faith in one God, and entered the Covenant Between the Parts.

anc-10.label: Isaiah the Prophet
anc-10.bio: One of the greatest literary prophets. His prophecies of destruction and consolation — 'Comfort, comfort My people' — accompany Israel through the generations.

anc-3.label: Jacob the Patriarch
anc-3.bio: Chosen of the Patriarchs and father of the twelve tribes. 'A wholesome man dwelling in tents' who went down to Egypt and laid the foundation of the house of Israel.

anc-9.label: King Solomon
anc-9.bio: The wisest of all men and builder of the First Temple. Composed Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.

sup-7.label: The Vilna Gaon (the Gra)
sup-7.bio: The Gaon of his generations in Lithuania. Toiled in Torah with extraordinary diligence, mastering revealed and hidden Torah, grammar and mathematics — father of the Lithuanian yeshiva world.

623.label: Rabbi Abbahu
623.bio: A third-generation Amora in the Land of Israel and head of the study house in Caesarea, a disciple of Rabbi Yochanan. He dealt with the Roman authorities on the Jews’ behalf, served as the city’s sole judge, preached against early Christianity and instituted the order of the shofar blasts on Rosh Hashanah. He was known for his humility.
623.core_concept: Torah leadership can combine halakhic authority, dialogue with the government and defence of the boundaries of faith without losing humility: "where penitents stand, the completely righteous cannot stand", and "the world endures only for the sake of one who makes himself as nothing".

624.label: Imma Shalom
624.bio: One of the few women of the Tannaitic literature mentioned by name: daughter of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the Elder, sister of Rabban Gamliel of Yavne and wife of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus. When her husband was excommunicated she acted to prevent a disaster in the Nasi’s house, and in the story of the philosopher she exposed a corrupt judge.
624.core_concept: Even when the halakhic system is right in its public needs, harm to the individual has a price: "the gates of wronging are not locked". Imma Shalom joins a family tradition ("so I have received from my father's father's house"), moral sensitivity and legal sophistication.

625.label: Rabbi Raphael Berdugo (the “Angel Raphael”)
625.bio: Head of the rabbinical court and spiritual leader of the Jews of Meknes, Morocco: halakhic authority, kabbalist and commentator, known as “the Angel Raphael”. He enacted ordinances for the poor and in the law of inheritance, and wrote responsa, glosses on the Shulchan Aruch, a commentary on the Torah, Talmud novellae and a rationalist commentary on the Talmud’s aggadot.
625.core_concept: Comprehensive leadership: independence in ruling from the sources, priority for the plain sense, a rational approach to aggadah and making the Torah accessible to the public in its own language, alongside holiness, abstinence and sensitivity to the weaker classes.

626.label: Rabbi Nathan Shapira of Jerusalem (HaNasi)
626.bio: Kabbalist, judge and leader of the Ashkenazi community of Jerusalem, born in Krakow. He travelled as an emissary to Italy, the Netherlands and Germany, and died around 1667. He edited and annotated the writings of the Ari (the “Glosses of the Ranash”) and wrote Tov HaAretz, Matzat Shimurim and Yayin HaMeshumar.
626.core_concept: Kabbalah does not stay in the books of mystery: it shapes custom and halakha, from Tikkun Chatzot to the prohibition of gentiles' wine. Editing and correcting the writings of the Ari are also part of this, so that the Ari's teaching is passed on accurately and in order.

627.label: Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon HaLevi Bokrat
627.bio: A Spanish sage of the generation of the Expulsion who settled in Tunis. He wrote Sefer HaZikaron (1507), a super-commentary on Rashi’s commentary on the Torah, translated the responsa of the Rif from Judeo-Arabic into Hebrew and wrote liturgical poems. The book was first printed only in 1845, by Shadal.
627.core_concept: Rashi's commentary rests on precision in the language of the verse and on the midrashim of the Sages, and Bokrat answers the objections of the Ramban and others in order to defend it. This defence preserves biblical interpretation after the Expulsion and joins the tradition of Ashkenaz and France with the Andalusian tradition.

628.label: Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi
628.bio: Grandson of the Rosh, born in Toledo, who settled in Jerusalem. His encyclopedic Shevilei Emunah (“Ten Paths”) joins Torah, Kabbalah, philosophy, astronomy, anatomy and medicine, and influenced the Shelah and Hasidic literature.
628.core_concept: Scientific and philosophical knowledge serves faith and does not compete with it: rational inquiry explains the created world, and on metaphysical questions such as the nature of the divine, the reasons for the commandments and reward, Kabbalah is the source of truth.

629.label: Miriam the Prophetess
629.bio: The prophetess, sister of Moses and Aaron, active already in the Egyptian bondage: she stood up to her father’s despair, watched over the infant Moses and led the women in the Song of the Sea. In the wilderness she is counted among the three leaders and the well is tied to her; her slander and its punishment became the basis of the commandment to remember what was done to Miriam.
629.core_concept: Faith is an action that prepares the vessels before the miracle comes: Miriam and the women brought drums out of Egypt and led song from below to above ("returning light"). Her leadership gave the people its existential foundation, and her absence at her death revealed how much the other leaders had leaned on her.

1.label: Ben Sira
1.bio: Shimon ben Yeshua ben Sira, one of the great sages of Jerusalem in Second Temple times, wrote his book around 180 BCE, as Hellenistic culture was reaching the upper classes of Judea. The book was not admitted to the canon, but the Sages quoted its finest sayings and wove them into midrash and prayer, and its lost Hebrew text was found again in the Cairo Geniza and at Masada.
1.core_concept: Supreme wisdom, which sought a dwelling among the nations, came to rest in Jerusalem, and it is the Torah of Moses; man chooses between good and evil, and his reward comes in this world and in the good name he leaves behind.

3.label: Philo of Alexandria
3.bio: A Hellenistic Jewish thinker who developed a systematic allegorical reading of Scripture and a synthesis with Greek philosophy; his influence flourished mainly among the Church Fathers.
3.core_concept: The Torah as a universal law of nature, and allegorical interpretation as a bridge between the commandments and wisdom.

345.label: Yehuda ben Tema
345.bio: A Tanna who educated towards spiritual courage, a sense of shame, and standing firm against social pressure.
345.core_concept: A balance between holy boldness and moral humility.

6.label: Aquila of Pontus
6.bio: Aquila of Pontus produced an extremely literal translation of Scripture to keep faith with the Hebrew original and to make room for the midrash of the Oral Torah. The translation was written against the Christian use of the Septuagint, and it also influenced Christian scholarship through Origen and the Hexapla. Its literalism also made it a key tool in the study of the biblical text.
6.core_concept: Translation as a shield of identity: a literalism that keeps faith with the Hebrew and leaves room for midrash, against Christian interpretation.

7.label: Rabbi Chiya the Great
7.bio: He saved the Torah from oblivion through comprehensive practical action. He combined physical and spiritual labour to hand down the tradition.
7.core_concept: The Torah is preserved by deeds. Personal responsibility for passing it on from generation to generation.

332.label: Midrash Rabbah
332.bio: A central midrashic corpus on the Torah and the Five Scrolls, edited over centuries, reflecting the spiritual world of the Sages.
332.core_concept: Turning Scripture into a living space of interpretation, ethics and awareness.

14.label: Rabbi Shimon Lavi
14.bio: A kabbalist, physician and poet who worked to build up the Jewry of Tripoli; he wrote a profound commentary on the Zohar and liturgical poems that took root throughout the Jewish world.
14.core_concept: The liturgical poem as a mystical-practical text: blurring reader and hero, and partnership in the experience of the Shekhinah's ascent.

201.label: Rabbi Elazar Birabi Kalir
201.bio: The greatest of the early liturgical poets, who shaped the language of prayer and piyyut for generations.
201.core_concept: Piyyut as a deep language of midrash, words and mystery.

21.label: Rav Sherira Gaon
21.bio: A founding document that for the first time sets out the chronological sequence of the Oral Torah from the Tannaim to the Geonim. It explains the editing of the Mishnah, the sealing of the Talmud and the role of the Savoraim, and establishes a rabbinic historical consciousness.
21.core_concept: Tradition as an authoritative historical narrative: the authority of the Oral Torah is also built by documenting its transmission and the order of the generations.

26.label: Rabbi Yonah ibn Janah
26.bio: He built the foundations of Hebrew grammar. A refugee who became a leading linguist and taught Hebrew as Torah.
26.core_concept: Precise Hebrew as understanding the word of God. The study of language is a mission of faith.

28.label: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Asher HaLevi (the First Riva)
28.bio: Student and son-in-law of R. Elyakim, one of the heads of the Speyer yeshiva and an initiator of the Tosafist method; he combined French and German traditions, engaged in trade, and gave complex halakhic rulings.
28.core_concept: Revolutionising study, from the beit midrash to broad dialectical interpretation; creating an analytical, logical approach.

261.label: Rabbi Meir ben Shmuel of Ramerupt
261.bio: Son-in-law of Rashi and father of Rabbenu Tam and the Rashbam, one of the figures who shaped the move from Rashi's direct explanation to Tosafist dialectic.
261.core_concept: Seeing the Talmud as one organic body and seeking conceptual consistency between sugyot and tractates.

32.label: Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash (the Ri Migash)
32.bio: Student of the Rif and head of the yeshiva of Lucena. He set the Talmud as the supreme authority and laid the foundation for the Rambam's halakhic study.
32.core_concept: Independent intellectual criticism of tradition; deep study and understanding above blind acceptance.

34.label: Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud (the First Ra'avad)
34.bio: Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud HaLevi (1110–1180) saw a double threat to rabbinic Judaism: Karaism from within and Aristotelian philosophy from without. In "Sefer HaKabbalah" he fortified the continuity of the Oral Torah, and in "HaEmunah HaRamah" he was the first to ground faith on Aristotelian foundations, paving the way for the Rambam.
34.core_concept: Torah and wisdom complete each other: history fortifies the authority of tradition, and reason grounds faith up to the point where it stops.

39.label: Rabbenu Bachya ibn Paquda (Duties of the Heart)
39.bio: The author of "Duties of the Heart" identifies a spiritual crisis: a religion of outward deeds without intention. He offers an orderly method of the service of the heart – faith, love, awe, trust and inner awareness.
39.core_concept: A distinction between the duties of the limbs and the duties of the heart: the deed matters – but intention and inner responsibility are the core of religious service.

45.label: Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor
45.bio: A student of Rabbenu Tam. A commentary on the Torah by precise plain sense, opposed to allegory. He combined a human, psychological reading with polemic against Christianity.
45.core_concept: Minimising miracles and preferring natural explanation; "double stories" as a description from two angles; a sharp defence of the Jewish plain sense against Christian allegory.

48.label: Benjamin of Tudela
48.bio: On his journey Benjamin of Tudela documented Jewish communities, their numbers and their social and political standing, drawing a rare map of the Diaspora. His descriptions point to the gap between prosperity under Muslim rule and oppression under Christian rule, and combine commercial information with popular traditions. The book became a central source for medieval Jewish history despite an editor's hand and legendary tales.
48.core_concept: Mapping the Diaspora as an ethos: documenting Jewish communities as a basis for historical memory and the consciousness of Jewish unity.

55.label: Yalkut Shimoni
55.bio: A vast midrashic anthology in the order of the verses of the Bible, preserving midrashim that were otherwise lost. It is attributed to Rabbi Shimon HaDarshan.
55.core_concept: Preservation rather than innovation – a spiritual archive of rabbinic thought. Keeping tradition alive precisely in an age of collapsing communities and persecution.

58.label: Rabbi Ephraim Ankawa
58.bio: A refugee of the decrees of 1391 who became rabbi of the city of Tlemcen, a physician and a liturgical poet. The story of the lion is tied to him, and his writings discuss miracles, nature and faith.
58.core_concept: Joining faith in miracles with a rational, philosophical reading (in the Maimonidean line) of the order of nature.

59.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Canpanton
59.bio: Canpanton founded a logical method of Gemara study that saved the world of Torah on the eve of the Expulsion.
59.core_concept: The way of study is the defence of the Torah: a logical, orderly method of studying the Gemara, in five stages and with rules against faulty reasoning, shows that scientific thinking and the Talmudic tradition do not contradict each other.

61.label: Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa
61.bio: Author of "Menorat HaMaor", written out of the pain of his generation and its spiritual dispersion. He gathered midrash, aggadah and the Zohar into a living, accessible path of ethics.
61.core_concept: Ethics as a "living melody": charity as repair and rescue; prayer as standing in poverty; building a life through stories and parables.

62.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab
62.bio: Author of "Menorat HaMaor" as a book of ethics for the whole people – women, children and craftsmen. He combined the Sages, aggadah and halakha into an educational picture.
62.core_concept: Bringing the "heart" back to the centre: intellect without ethics is not enough; every commandment and good trait sheds an inner light.

65.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Arama (the Ba'al ha-Akedah)
65.bio: One of the great thinkers of 15th-century Spanish Jewry (1420–1494), a rabbi, preacher and head of a yeshiva. In his book "Akedat Yitzchak" he developed a three-stage method of homily that answered Christianity and extreme Aristotelian philosophy and strengthened the faith of the educated on the eve of the Expulsion.
65.core_concept: The homily as a stronghold of faith: joining reason, biblical interpretation and Kabbalah to build spiritual resilience in an age of crisis.

66.label: Rabbi Eliyahu Mizrachi (the Re'em)
66.bio: His logical, profound commentary on Rashi became the basis for understanding Rashi's interpretation; a spiritual leader of the Jewry of Constantinople.
66.core_concept: There is no superfluous word in Rashi – every word comes to answer a precise question. Building a systematic method of interpreting Rashi.

68.label: Rabbi Yosef Taitazak
68.bio: Head of a yeshiva and kabbalist among the exiles from Spain; author or receiver of the "Maggid" teachings and a central link in the generation of Safed and Salonica. He combined asceticism, an awareness of the End and a national vision.
68.core_concept: An active awareness of redemption and a vision of the return to Zion out of the kabbalistic world of the exiles from Spain.

71.label: Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak)
71.bio: One of the greatest kabbalists of Safed, who organised Kabbalah into an orderly theological system and built an ethical approach to imitating God.
71.core_concept: Shaping Kabbalah systematically and making it a practical, ethical path of repair for the person and the world.

73.label: Rabbi Mordechai Yaffe (the Ba'al ha-Levushim)
73.bio: A halakhic authority and leader who headed the Council of Four Lands and led national ordinances. He wrote "the Levushim" – a halakhic code that balances the length of the Beit Yosef against the brevity of the Shulchan Arukh, with sources and customs.
73.core_concept: Halakha as a "garment" for reality: an applied code that balances depth and accessibility and carries a broad public responsibility.

329.label: The Maharsha
329.bio: One of the great commentators on the Talmud and aggadah, a public leader and member of the Council of Four Lands. He shaped the yeshiva way of study and combined moral and public responsibility.
329.core_concept: Combining scholarly precision, aggadic depth and public responsibility.

77.label: Rabbi Avraham Azulai
77.bio: Azulai went up to the Land of Israel and built an orderly kabbalistic system resting on the Ari and the Ramak. In "Chesed LeAvraham" he draws a map of reality: there is no chance, man is responsible as a "small world", the Shekhinah is in exile, and repair comes through the commandments, Gehinnom and reincarnation. He stresses a metaphysical distinction between the Land of Israel and the lands outside it, and had great influence through the Chida and his own descendants.
77.core_concept: There is no chance: a kabbalistic map of reality that sets man as the repairer of the world, and the Land of Israel as the realm of direct providence.

78.label: Rabbi Yehuda Aryeh of Modena
78.bio: Rabbi Yehuda Aryeh of Modena was a rabbi, preacher and polemicist in the Venice ghetto, a linguistic genius and a prolific writer. Alongside a broad spiritual enterprise, he honestly recorded his gambling addiction and his failings in the autobiography "Chayei Yehuda". His writings range from defending tradition to sharp criticism of Kabbalah and dialogue with the Christian world.
78.core_concept: Spiritual honesty as a model of leadership: genius alongside a candid exposure of weakness and inner struggle.

79.label: Rabbi David HaLevi Segal (the Taz)
79.bio: An important halakhic authority who wrote the "Turei Zahav", lived a life of wandering and suffering, shaped Ashkenazi halakha, and remains a revered figure in tradition and in Hasidism.
79.core_concept: Halakha as life – thoughtful, sensitive to custom, full of faith. Labour for the truth out of suffering and humility.

80.label: Rabbi Shalom Shabazi
80.bio: Rabbi Shalom Shabazi was a Yemenite liturgical poet and kabbalist who lived in a generation of decrees, poverty and exile. He led his community in times of crisis too, and wrote poems of redemption and hope out of the exile of Mawza. His poetry crossed borders, from the Tiklal and synagogue tradition to Israeli music, and set a model of combining Maimonidean loyalty with a rich world of mystery.
80.core_concept: Liturgical poetry as a force of leadership and theology: combining the Rambam with the world of mystery and turning exile into hope.

82.label: Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas
82.bio: Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas (1610–1698), born in Oran in Algeria and a descendant of Nahmanides, headed the rabbinical court of Tlemcen as a young man, then moved between North Africa, Amsterdam, London, Hamburg and Livorno until he became chief rabbi of the Sephardic community of Amsterdam. In the years of Shabbetai Tzvi he stood almost alone against the messianic frenzy, and gathered the letters of that struggle in "Tzitzat Novel Tzvi".
82.core_concept: Torah authority comes not from visions or charisma but from submission to halakha and to the tradition of rulings; true Kabbalah upholds the commandments, and a Kabbalah that breaks them is strange fire.

83.label: Rabbi Shabtai HaKohen (the Shach)
83.bio: A brilliant halakhic authority who demanded a fresh opening of halakha, challenged received opinion, innovated in study, and whose books became a foundation of study and ruling to this day.
83.core_concept: Halakha as open inquiry, not a closed collection; innovative principles in monetary law and in doubts.

84.label: Rabbi Avraham Abele Gombiner (the Magen Avraham)
84.bio: An important halakhic authority whose commentary on the Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chaim, was accepted as law. He brought Kabbalah into halakhic ruling, and the halakhic times of day are reckoned according to him.
84.core_concept: Bringing kabbalistic depth into settled halakha; short, clear rulings with influence across the generations.

86.label: Rabbi Moshe Hagiz
86.bio: After the trauma of Sabbateanism, Hagiz acted as a responsible zealot, setting boundaries against what he saw as the disintegration of tradition. A personal crisis led him to devote himself to writing and polemic, and to clashes that echoed through the communities of Europe. In "Leket HaKemach" he sought to draw up a renewed order and restore a central halakhic authority, even at the cost of polarisation and dispute.
86.core_concept: Zeal as responsibility: drawing boundaries to prevent spiritual collapse after Sabbateanism – at a high price.

88.label: Rabbi Yisrael Yaakov Algazi
88.bio: Head of the Beit El yeshiva and a leader of Jerusalem; he wrote dozens of books and combined public responsibility with kabbalistic depth.
88.core_concept: A Torah that joins the revealed and the hidden, and the beit midrash with the welfare of the community.

89.label: Rabbi Yaakov Emden (the Yaavetz)
89.bio: One of the great sages of 18th-century Ashkenaz, son and student of the "Chacham Tzvi". He kept away from official rabbinic posts to preserve his independence, combined bold halakhic innovation with textual criticism and openness to science, and fought Sabbateanism, including the amulets controversy against Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschütz.
89.core_concept: Spiritual independence as a condition of truth: bold ruling, philological precision and an uncompromising stand against Sabbateanism.

90.label: Rabbi Moshe David Valle (the Ramad Valle)
90.bio: A qualified physician and close friend of the Ramchal. He developed a method of interpretation: the plain sense itself hints at mystery in every grammatical or linguistic change.
90.core_concept: Mapping the language of Scripture onto the structure of the sefirot; rejecting outside wisdoms as a substitute; a vast body of commentary revealed only in recent generations.

91.label: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Ginzburg (the Sha'agat Aryeh)
91.bio: A Talmudic genius and independent halakhic authority who lived in poverty and wandering, clashed with the establishment and was not afraid to disagree. His book "Sha'agat Aryeh" became a cornerstone of rulings on Orach Chaim, and his works are studied in depth.
91.core_concept: Halakhic truth without compromise: precision in the sources of the Rishonim and independence in ruling – even at the price of public solitude.

93.label: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto (the Ramchal)
93.bio: A young genius who endured disputes and bans. "Mesillat Yesharim" became a foundational book of ethics; he wrote a kabbalistic-philosophical system of the philosophy of history.
93.core_concept: Kabbalah as a map of divine governance and redemption; building a precise spiritual ladder; holiness as entering reality, not escaping it.

95.label: The Noda bi-Yehuda (Rabbi Yechezkel Landau)
95.bio: A central halakhic authority in Eastern Europe and author of the "Noda bi-Yehuda". He faced the challenges of the Haskalah while preserving a sharp halakhic tradition.
95.core_concept: Upholding the tradition of halakha while facing the challenges of the time out of public responsibility.

96.label: Rabbi Shalom Sharabi (the Rashash)
96.bio: The Rashash organised the teaching of the Ari into a precise system and became the leader of Kabbalah in Jerusalem.
96.core_concept: Prayer is an act of repair: the kavanot he arranged according to the teaching of the Ari turn every word of prayer into a unification of worlds, and unite communities around a shared spiritual service.

97.label: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Heller (the Ketzot ha-Choshen)
97.bio: The author of the "Ketzot HaChoshen" as an innovator of scholarship: precise concepts in monetary law, sharp argument and an enormous influence on the yeshiva world.
97.core_concept: The inner logic of halakha: clarifying definitions creates legal and moral clarity at once.

98.label: Rabbi Avraham Danzig
98.bio: A halakhic authority and author of "Chayei Adam" and "Chochmat Adam". He wrote clear, practical guides to halakha for householders, out of his own experience as a working man.
98.core_concept: An accessible system of halakha by rules, distinctions between degrees of obligation, and a separation between books of study and practical halakha.

99.label: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin
99.bio: A student of the Vilna Gaon and founder of the Volozhin yeshiva. In "Nefesh HaChaim" he presents a theology of Torah as a cosmic engine and a model of devotion.
99.core_concept: Torah study as the force that sustains reality; devotion through study, and the institutional system of the modern yeshiva.

100.label: Menachem Mendel Lefin (of Satanov)
100.bio: A maskil and rabbi who formed a practical method for improving character traits through a daily moral journal, and deeply influenced the Mussar movement through Rabbi Israel Salanter's edition.
100.core_concept: Systematic, measured work on character traits (a daily journal of traits) as a moderate "religious enlightenment" loyal to the Torah.

102.label: The Chatam Sofer (Rabbi Moshe Sofer)
102.bio: The father of modern Orthodoxy, a fierce opponent of Reform. He made the principle "the new is forbidden by the Torah" a comprehensive ideology.
102.core_concept: Conservatism as an essential response to modernity; strengthening tradition and custom against the dissolution of Jewish identity.

103.label: Rabbi Chaim Palagi (the Chabif)
