103.bio: A halakhic authority and leader who founded charitable and educational institutions, set communal ordinances, and left an enormous body of writing despite losing manuscripts in a fire.
103.core_concept: Halakha as social leadership: ethics, peace and education as a binding public system.

104.label: Rabbi Yehuda Bibas
104.bio: A rabbi and thinker who advanced redemption by human action; influenced by the nationalist spirit of his time, he called for a national and political awakening, and influenced his student R. Yehuda Alkalai.
104.core_concept: Repentance as a "political return" – a move from passive expectation to historical action.

105.label: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer
105.bio: A conservative halakhic authority who drew up a practical plan for redemption: immigration, agriculture and building the Land "little by little". He proposed bold halakhic steps (such as discussing the renewal of the sacrifices) and worked with philanthropists and powers.
105.core_concept: Redemption little by little: human responsibility as a commandment – national initiative without cutting loose from halakha.

108.label: Rabbi Yehuda Alkalai
108.bio: An early religious-Zionist thinker who reads "repentance" as a national process: the return to the Land is itself the redemption. He proposes a plan of action: economic companies, political initiatives and national unity around Hebrew and a single identity.
108.core_concept: General repentance means return: historical responsibility passes from heaven to man and to the community.

110.label: Shadal (Samuel David Luzzatto)
110.bio: Shadal argued that authentic Judaism is a religion of compassion and faith, not of cold reason, and built a scholarly enterprise (language, Bible, textual criticism) to defend the vitality of tradition. He fought the circles of Wissenschaft des Judentums, which seemed to him to turn Judaism into archaeology, and attacked the introduction of "Greek wisdom" into Judaism. The pain of his life strengthened in him the supremacy of faith and good deeds.
110.core_concept: Defending a Judaism of compassion and faith against cold rationalism – through the study of Bible and language.

112.label: Rabbi Yaakov Abuhatzeira
112.bio: A prominent kabbalist and halakhic authority from Morocco, a spiritual leader known for his asceticism and his greatness in Torah. His influence is felt to this day in the Abuhatzeira dynasty.
112.core_concept: Joining Kabbalah and halakha out of humility; personal and social repair as the purpose of the Torah.

114.label: Adolphe Franck
114.bio: A German-born scholar who sought to present Kabbalah as a profound philosophical theology – not an inferior mysticism.
114.core_concept: Kabbalah as a form of metaphysical thought with universal religious meaning.

116.label: The Maharil Diskin
116.bio: Founder of the Haredi model of leadership in Jerusalem, a fierce opponent of the Haskalah, who worked to establish institutions of Torah and welfare.
116.core_concept: Building Haredi autonomy, combining firmness in ruling with the building of supporting institutions.

117.label: Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin
117.bio: A Lithuanian prodigy who became a Hasid after meeting R. Mordechai Yosef of Izbica. He offers a theology in which the Oral Torah is an ongoing revelation through human struggle, and doubt is a condition of deep discovery.
117.core_concept: The fall as part of the process: sin and repentance are read backwards as part of God's will; the real danger is despair.

118.label: Elijah Benamozegh
118.bio: Benamozegh presented Kabbalah as the heart of Judaism and as a system able to interpret and critique modernity (from Spinoza to Kant and Darwin). He formulated a two-storey vision: Israel as keeper of the Torah of Moses, and the Noahide laws as a universal goal for humanity. Though rejected by rival camps, in recent generations he has been rediscovered as offering a modernity of integration rather than rupture.
118.core_concept: Kabbalah as Jewish universalism: joining the tradition of mystery with modern philosophy and the Noahide vision.

120.label: Rabbi Shmuel Mohliver
120.bio: A leader of Hibbat Zion who understood that the return to the Land is a practical task. He bridged religious and secular Jews, worked with Rothschild to found settlements, and supported the sale permit in the shmita controversy to save the settlement.
120.core_concept: A broad public alliance as a redemptive need: unity among different forces in the people in order to build reality.

123.label: The Arukh HaShulchan (Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein)
123.bio: Author of the "Arukh HaShulchan" series of halakhic books, which set out the entire Shulchan Arukh in an innovative, summarising approach.
123.core_concept: Presenting halakha as a living, contemporary entity with authority that comes from its roots.

342.label: Rabbi Chaim Chizkiyahu Medini
342.bio: Author of the halakhic encyclopedia "Sdei Chemed", which gathered the halakhic literature of many generations.
342.core_concept: Order and clarity in a vast and scattered halakhic world.

129.label: The Sefat Emet
129.bio: The Rebbe of Ger and one of the great thinkers of Hasidism. He created a mystical-existential language of exile as concealment and redemption as revelation.
129.core_concept: "The inner point" as a tool for serving God and for reading reality: raising light out of darkness.

131.label: Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain (the Shem MiShmuel)
131.bio: A central Hasidic rebbe and thinker; his sermons combine mystery, spiritual psychology and the improvement of character.
131.core_concept: The concept of "surrounding lights", and a deeper look at inner will, inadvertent sin, and a unity that does not erase the individual.

132.label: Rabbi Yosef Rosen (the Rogatchover Gaon)
132.bio: "One of a kind in his generation", who lived with the Talmud and the Rambam, read the Rambam as a single whole, and brought philosophical tools to the understanding of halakha; his manuscripts were saved and became the basis of a printing enterprise in later generations.
132.core_concept: Reading the Rambam as an "overarching system" that unites halakha, aggadah and conceptual study under one Torah.

133.label: Rabbi Yehuda Moshe Yeshua Fatiya
133.bio: A student of the Babylonian tradition who made the Ari's system accessible in a clear exposition and wrote central works; he is also known for traditions of repairing souls and for prayers during the Second World War.
133.core_concept: The study of mystery as a "purifying obligation" that brings redemption closer and protects the soul – even without full understanding.

135.label: Hillel Zeitlin
135.bio: Hillel Zeitlin: a Jewish philosopher between Nietzsche and Hasidism, a cultural critic who returned to spiritual depth; he was murdered in the Holocaust.
135.core_concept: The search itself is the service of God: turning doubt and modernity into an engine of repentance and spiritual renewal.

136.label: Rabbi Khalfon Moshe HaKohen
136.bio: Rabbi Khalfon Moshe HaKohen as rabbi of Djerba: extensive halakhic writing, public responsibility, and a link between local tradition and national consciousness.
136.core_concept: Halakha as an engine of leadership: holiness that translates into communal mutual responsibility and a vision of the return to Zion.

138.label: Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Chai Uziel
138.bio: A Rishon LeZion and far-sighted halakhic authority who worked for the unity of the Yishuv and the state, developed a realistic public halakha, and cooperated historically with Rabbi Herzog.
138.core_concept: National and public halakha: combining Maimonidean rationality with social responsibility and unity.

139.label: Rabbi Yaakov Moshe Charlap
139.bio: Rabbi Charlap as a student and colleague of Rabbi Kook: a language of repentance and redemption, a link between Kabbalah and national action, and influence in Jerusalem.
139.core_concept: Redemption as a spiritual and national process: repairing character and society is part of sovereignty.

140.label: Rabbi Aryeh Levin
140.bio: An exceptional moral figure in Jerusalem, the rabbi of the prisoners, a symbol of humility and practical holiness.
140.core_concept: Kindness as a way of life. A revolutionary humility in a changing world.

141.label: Franz Rosenzweig
141.bio: In "The Star of Redemption" he dismantles the "totality" and proposes a structure of God, man and world through creation, revelation and redemption. He founded the Lehrhaus in Frankfurt and translated the Bible with Buber, while coping with ALS.
141.core_concept: Revelation as speech and love that give birth to responsibility; truth is created in encounter, not in an abstract system.

143.label: The Rebbe of Piaseczno
143.bio: A portrait of the Rebbe of Piaseczno as educator and thinker: Hasidic depth, an understanding of the soul, and the courage to go on teaching and writing inside the Warsaw Ghetto.
143.core_concept: Holiness that refuses to flee: the service of God is built out of inner truth even when reality collapses.

144.label: Rabbi Ovadia Hadaya
144.bio: A halakhic authority and kabbalist who saw the founding of the State as a divine act. He supported Zionism not as a compromise but as a revelation of redemption.
144.core_concept: Kabbalah that does not flee reality but acts within it; redemption as a political and mystical process.

147.label: Rabbi Yosef Messas
147.bio: A polymath who saw reality as a tool for understanding halakha, ruled boldly out of compassion and the spirit of the time, and strengthened the unity of Israel between exile and rebirth.
147.core_concept: An eternal halakha that meets time: halakhic realism as the key to preserving tradition in a changing society.

149.label: Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim
149.bio: Rishon LeZion and Chief Rabbi of Israel; he led a statesmanlike and independent line, worked to bring the distant close, and took firm public positions.
149.core_concept: A proud and independent state rabbinate – combining leadership, ruling and national responsibility.

152.label: Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel
152.bio: A thinker who joined Hasidism and philosophy with public ethics. He wrote "The Sabbath" and "The Prophets", was active in civil rights, and marched alongside Martin Luther King – "praying with my legs".
152.core_concept: The holiness of time and wonder as the engine of faith; moral responsibility as an inseparable part of the service of God.

155.label: Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli
155.bio: Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli created a new halakhic language for questions of sovereignty: state, army, law and ethics, with deep study and a readiness to innovate. He dealt with questions such as rescue operations, the ransom of soldiers, shmita and medicine, and was also a sharp critic of religious politicisation. The chapter presents a halakhic authority who joins the beit midrash to national reality with responsibility.
155.core_concept: A halakha of sovereignty: developing a halakhic language for state, army and law out of bold study and moral responsibility.

156.label: Rabbi Pinchas Kehati
156.bio: Author of "Mishnayot Kehati" – a clear, educational commentary written out of an educational mission to the wider public.
156.core_concept: Making the Mishnah accessible in modern, systematic language – a bridge between the beit midrash and the public.

157.label: Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach
157.bio: The halakhic authority of the generation, in shining modesty. He studied modern reality, and his rulings changed whole areas of life.
157.core_concept: Halakha out of moral responsibility, in dialogue with modern reality rather than cut off from it.

158.label: The Slonimer Rebbe (the Netivot Shalom)
158.bio: A rebbe and educator who rebuilt a Hasidic world after the Holocaust, and developed an accessible spiritual language of faith, atmosphere and education.
158.core_concept: An educational "atmosphere" as a builder of identity; faith and trust as a force that creates reality in the generation of rebirth.

159.label: Rabbi Moshe-Zvi Neria
159.bio: Neria, a student of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, founded the Kfar HaRoeh yeshiva and was one of the leaders of Bnei Akiva, building the foundations of religious-Zionist education. He educated through personal connection, mission and the primacy of action, and saw the building of Torah institutions as a response to the destruction of Europe. The chapter also presents his complexity regarding army service and the tension between the ideal "royal road" and practical responsibility after the fact.
159.core_concept: "After the fact" as a mission: an educational revolution out of personal example and a sense of national responsibility.

160.label: Rabbi Shmuel HaLevi Wosner
160.bio: Author of the responsa "Shevet HaLevi" and head of the Chachmei Lublin yeshiva. He led a community and ruled decisively in an age of technological change.
160.core_concept: Standing firm against modernity out of deep tradition and consistency in ruling.

161.label: André Neher
161.bio: A French Jewish thinker who dealt with the meaning of Judaism after the Holocaust. He saw in God's silence a call to human responsibility.
161.core_concept: Judaism as an invitation to create meaning in a silent world; the holiness of the everyday and of moral action.

163.label: Éliane Amado Lévy-Valensi
163.bio: A profound thinker who joined Bible, philosophy and psychoanalysis. She saw Abraham as an existential figure of responsibility and history.
163.core_concept: The Abrahamic being – man as a moral presence who creates history by saying "Here I am".

164.label: Rabbi Levi Saadia Nahmani
164.bio: A kabbalist and scribe. Warnings and predictions are attributed to him (the Six-Day War, Yom Kippur). He stressed active redemption: prayer, unity and calling for the Messiah.
164.core_concept: The outer struggle as an inner mirror; a demand for repair and unity between religious and secular; "there is no Messiah unless we ask for him".

165.label: Rabbi Meir Zeini
165.bio: Rabbi of communities in Algeria and a military chaplain; in France he revived a synagogue and passed on a Livornese and Zionist identity. He moved to Israel at the age of 85.
165.core_concept: The leadership of "the great and mighty" that joins Torah and action; redemption out of the meeting of prayer and deed, and preserving the melody of tradition.

167.label: Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz
167.bio: Rabbi of the Western Wall and head of the Beit El (kabbalists') yeshiva; he combined hidden service with practical management and sensitivity to all of Israel.
167.core_concept: A living bridge between deep holiness and public, national responsibility at the holiest and most sensitive place in the world.

168.label: Rabbi Chaim David HaLevi
168.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities and thinkers of the State of Israel, and from 5733 (1972–73) until his death the Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv–Jaffa. He combined loyalty to the Sephardi tradition of ruling with a Zionism that sees Jewish sovereignty as a stage of redemption, and saw halakha as a living system, as his book "Aseh Lecha Rav" and his ruling forbidding smoking show.
168.core_concept: A living, purposeful halakha that answers the challenges of modernity, medicine and technology, seeing the State as a stage in the process of redemption.

170.label: Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky
170.bio: Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky as a model of diligence and ruling: extensive writings, broad public influence and a unique standing among the Lithuanian community.
170.core_concept: Authority built from perseverance: spiritual power without show, out of daily loyalty to the Torah.

173.label: Rabbi Chaim Druckman
173.bio: A Holocaust survivor who became a central leader of religious Zionism: head of the Or Etzion institutions, a leader of Bnei Akiva and president of the hesder yeshivot. He bore responsibility for the state conversion system out of love of Israel.
173.core_concept: Responsible leadership that holds Torah, army and state together, with an emphasis on unity and love of people.

176.label: Rabbi Avichai Rontzki
176.bio: A fighter and company commander in the Shaked reconnaissance unit who turned to the world of Torah after the Yom Kippur War. He helped found the Elon Moreh yeshiva, was one of the founders of the settlement of Itamar and founded its yeshiva, and until 2010 was the fifth Chief Military Rabbi of the IDF.
176.core_concept: Combining military, Torah and settlement leadership: fighting spirit grows from a Zionism connected to the roots of the Torah and the Land.

177.label: Rabbi Elisha Wishlitzky
177.bio: An educator and grassroots leader who connected communities and streams, stressed relations between people as the foremost religious measure, and set out a language of generosity and mission.
177.core_concept: Leadership of connection: humility as working strength, truth wrapped in love and listening.

178.label: The Kabbalah as Adolphe Franck Saw It (1843)
178.bio: A survey of the development of Kabbalah from ancient traditions to the Zohar and the Ari, presenting the academic project of Adolphe Franck, who saw Kabbalah as a sophisticated philosophical-religious system. It highlights concepts such as Ein Sof, sefirot, kelippot and tikkun.
178.core_concept: Kabbalah as an all-explaining system: cosmology, theodicy and tikkun – and also as an engine of a tradition's inner development.

179.label: The Abuhatzeira Dynasty
179.bio: A dynasty of kabbalists that led Moroccan Jewry spiritually. A combination of holiness, humility and sublime liturgical poetry.
179.core_concept: Practical holiness alongside poems of redemption. Spiritual leadership through experience and tradition.

180.label: Chacham Tzion Chaviv Bracha
180.bio: Chacham Tzion Chaviv Bracha (d. 14 Tishrei 5765, 2004), an orphan from Aleppo who came to the Land of Israel as a boy, was a hidden Kabbalist in Jerusalem, a disciple of Rabbi Yehuda Fatiya and Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi. He earned his living as a greengrocer in the Machane Yehuda market and as a postman, and in 1970 founded the Leshem yeshiva in Nachlaot, where he chose to sit with the beginners and the newly observant.
180.core_concept: Leshem, "le-hakamat Shekhinta me-afra" (for raising the Shekhinah from the dust): at the centre stand the repair of the Shekhinah and of the whole people, not only the needs of the individual, carried out with love for every Jew, with humility and simplicity, and by accepting suffering as atonement for the generation.

331.label: The Expulsion from Spain
331.bio: A defining event in Jewish history that scattered the communities of Spain and led to new Jewish centres around the world.
331.core_concept: Preserving identity and memory even after the loss of a homeland.

183.label: The Zohar: Who Wrote It?
183.bio: The controversy over attributing the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai against claims of a later author, and what the question means for the authority of Kabbalah and the reading of the text.
183.core_concept: Beyond "who wrote it": how a text becomes canonical, and the responsibility of interpretation where tradition and history meet.

191.label: Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk
191.bio: One of the Hasidic leaders who went up to the Land of Israel and founded a community in Tiberias, with vision and spiritual connection.
191.core_concept: A vision of redemption through settling the Land, and leadership out of humility and devotion.

9.label: The Septuagint
9.bio: A defining event in which the Torah was first translated into Greek. It stirred religious and cultural controversy between Judaism, Christianity and Hellenistic culture.
9.core_concept: Translation as a dangerous tool or a bridge. How language changes the meaning of a sacred text.

193.label: Shimon Kefa (Simon Peter)
193.bio: The chapter presents the gap between the Christian tradition about Peter and Jewish traditions that portray Shimon Kefa as a hidden emissary meant to separate Judaism from Christianity in order to prevent bloodshed and assimilation. According to the story, he shaped customs and a theology that set Christianity apart from Judaism, while studying Torah in secret. Liturgical attributions and traditions around the fast of the Tenth of Tevet are also presented.
193.core_concept: Traditions as a mechanism of identity: the story of a "hidden emissary" that reads a religious split as a defensive step by the community.

197.label: Rabbi Meir Kahane
197.bio: A rabbi, ideologue and activist who placed the question of the State's Jewish identity at the centre.
197.core_concept: Placing the Torah and Jewish identity at the heart of public and political debate.

199.label: Rabbi Refael Immanuel Chai Ricchi
199.bio: A kabbalist, liturgical poet and commentator on the Mishnah, one of the prominent figures of Italian Kabbalah.
199.core_concept: Combining the Kabbalah of the Ari with systematic teaching and halakhic-kabbalistic literature.

346.label: Rabbi Elazar ben Arach
346.bio: One of the greatest students of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, known as "the ever-flowing spring" and for the teaching of "a good heart".
346.core_concept: Creativity in Torah requires a bond with the community and the fellowship.

349.label: Rabbi David Pardo
349.bio: One of the great commentators on the Tosefta, who brought its study back to the centre of the beit midrash through his commentary "Chasdei David".
349.core_concept: Textual precision alongside a deep commitment to tradition.

350.label: Rav Evyatar ben Eliyahu HaKohen
350.bio: One of the last Geonim of the Land of Israel, who fought to preserve the spiritual authority of the Land against the centres of Babylonia.
350.core_concept: Spiritual independence and the holiness of the Land of Israel as a source of authority.

352.label: Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Ghiyyat
352.bio: One of the great sages of Spain and continuers of the Geonic tradition, a halakhic authority, poet and head of the yeshiva in Lucena.
352.core_concept: A link between the tradition of Babylonia and the Golden Age of Spain.

353.label: Rabbenu Yitzchak ben Yehuda of Mainz
353.bio: Head of the Mainz yeshiva and Rashi's principal teacher, one of the shapers of the Ashkenazi method of study.
353.core_concept: Combining textual precision, custom and ruling.

355.label: Rabbi Yehuda ben Natan (the Rivan)
355.bio: Rashi's son-in-law and continuer, who served as a central link between Rashi's commentaries and the Tosafists.
355.core_concept: Innovation out of loyalty to tradition.

356.label: Machzor Vitry
356.bio: A halakhic and liturgical encyclopedia from Rashi's school, preserving the French rite and early Ashkenazi traditions.
356.core_concept: Joining prayer, halakha, aggadah and community life.

265.label: Rabbi Shemaria of Speyer
265.bio: One of the first Tosafists in Ashkenaz and a key figure in the Speyer community. He helped shape the dialectical method of study, fixed liturgical traditions and led a community under persecution.
265.core_concept: Combining Tosafist scholarly creativity with deep loyalty to the customs of Ashkenaz and to shaping community life and prayer.

268.label: Queen Esther
268.bio: A central biblical figure who went from a hidden woman in a foreign palace to a leader who saved her people. Her story presents leadership that acts from concealment, with wisdom, timing and national responsibility.
268.core_concept: A model of leadership from hiddenness – wise, patient and well-timed action within existing systems of power to save the whole.

269.label: Queen Helena
269.bio: The queen of Adiabene, who chose to bind her fate to the people of Israel and to Jerusalem. She is known for her conversion, her generosity in the years of famine, her gifts to the Temple and her standing in rabbinic literature.
269.core_concept: Turning foreign royal power into a deep commitment to the Torah, to kindness and to the life of Jerusalem, to the point of joining the nation's halakhic and spiritual world.

270.label: Huldah the Prophetess
270.bio: A prophetess in Jerusalem in the days of King Josiah, to whom the king and the High Priest turned after the book of the Torah was found in the Temple. Her prophetic confirmation places her at the point of transition between living prophecy and the authority of the written Torah.
270.core_concept: Confirming the authority of the sacred text through prophecy, and setting a woman as the supreme spiritual authority at a decisive moment.

272.label: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Yaakov HaLavan of Prague
272.bio: One of the prominent figures of the generation of Rishonim in Bohemia and Ashkenaz, who studied with Rabbenu Tam and the Riva. He created a bridge between the Torah centres of France and Ashkenaz and established Prague as an important centre of Torah.
272.core_concept: Combining the sharpness of the French Tosafot with practical Ashkenazi ruling, while creating a pan-European network of influence.

274.label: Abigail
274.bio: One of the impressive figures of the Bible, who stopped David in a moment of anger and prevented bloodshed. In a short, precise speech she brought him back to his moral and royal calling.
274.core_concept: The power of sober moral speech to stop a leader at a moment of danger and return him to his calling and his historical responsibility.

277.label: Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui
277.bio: One of the great sages of Tlemcen, who acted as a halakhic authority, liturgical poet and community leader, alongside notable scientific work. In his book "Moneh Mispar" he made mathematics accessible in Hebrew for halakhic and communal needs.
277.core_concept: Combining science and mathematics as tools for the service of God and for running a community, out of loyalty to halakha and Jewish rationalism.

278.label: Rabbi Yehonatan HaKohen of Lunel
278.bio: One of the great sages of Provence, whose commentary on the Rif made study accessible to generations of students in Europe. He was among the first to recognise the depth of the Rambam's system and corresponded with him.
278.core_concept: Building a bridge between Ashkenaz, Spain and Provence, spreading the Rambam's system and making the Rif and the Mishnah accessible to the learners of Europe.

281.label: Queen Shlomtzion (Salome Alexandra)
281.bio: Queen of Judea in the Hasmonean period, who restored stability to a divided kingdom through internal reconciliation, strengthening the Torah sages and political fortification.
281.core_concept: Combining spiritual, Torah leadership with political realism, building institutions and strengthening society instead of relying on wars of conquest.

282.label: Hannah the Prophetess
282.bio: A revolutionary biblical figure who turned prayer from an outward service into an inner pouring out of the soul before God. Her prayer and song became a foundational source for the laws of prayer.
282.core_concept: Establishing inner prayer as service of the heart, and turning personal pain into a national prophecy about kingship, history and the repair of the world.

273.label: Rabbi Eliezer ben Natan (the Ra'avan)
273.bio: One of the pillars of 12th-century Ashkenazi Jewry, who as a child lived through the horrors of the Crusades and became both an important halakhic authority and a central chronicler of the destruction.
273.core_concept: Turning the memory of destruction into a foundation of halakhic and spiritual building, with deep loyalty to the tradition of the Rishonim and the customs of Ashkenaz.

289.label: Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak)
289.bio: One of the great Bible commentators and grammarians, known as "the head of the grammarians". He turned complex Spanish grammatical theory into a clear method accessible to Torah learners in Europe.
289.core_concept: Combining linguistic precision, plain sense, historical understanding and loyalty to tradition as a central tool for grasping the depth of Scripture.

293.label: Rabbi Meir HaLevi Abulafia
293.bio: A halakhic authority, head of a yeshiva and a nasi with public authority in Toledo. He dealt with ruling, leadership, polemic over faith and the exact text of the Torah scroll down to the last letter.
293.core_concept: Guarding the halakhic tradition and the textual tradition against extreme philosophy and the undermining of the foundations of faith.

299.label: Tzidkiyah ben Avraham
299.bio: An Italian halakhic authority of the Anav family, who joined Ashkenazi tradition, Italian ruling and medical knowledge. His book "Shibbolei HaLeket" arranged the Jewish way of life in an accessible and systematic form.
299.core_concept: An Italian halakhic codification that joins diverse traditions out of humility, order and public responsibility.

403.label: The Riaz (Rabbi Isaiah ben Elijah di Trani)
403.bio: Grandson of the Rid the Elder, an independent halakhic authority who opposed making faith depend on philosophy and stressed the power of tradition.
403.core_concept: Loyalty to tradition alongside independence of thought.

302.label: Rabbi Estori HaParchi
302.bio: A scholar who walked the Land in person in order to understand halakha, and made the first halakhic mapping of the Land of Israel.
302.core_concept: Joining the Torah to the physical reality of the Land.

303.label: Rabbi Yitzchak of Corbeil (the Semak)
303.bio: Author of an accessible book of commandments that turned halakha into an everyday guide to life for every Jew.
303.core_concept: Making halakha a practical educational tool for the whole people.

406.label: Rabbenu Peretz of Corbeil
406.bio: One of the leaders of the later Tosafists and a central editor of the traditions of study and halakha in France.
406.core_concept: Preserving and organising the Torah tradition in a time of crisis.

408.label: Rabbi Eliezer of Touques
408.bio: Editor of the version of the Tosafot that was accepted in the printed Talmud and became the foundation of Gemara study for generations.
408.core_concept: Clarity and order as the key to passing on the tradition.

307.label: The Rivevan (Rabbi Yehuda ben Binyamin HaAnav)
307.bio: A central sage of Italian Jewry who established an independent halakhic tradition and preserved the customs of Rome, combining Talmudic depth with interpretive precision.
307.core_concept: Combining living tradition with a systematic interpretation of halakha.

312.label: Rabbi Moshe of Évreux
312.bio: A Tosafist who developed a revolutionary conception: the books themselves are the source of authority, and the learner is an active partner in interpretation.
312.core_concept: "The book as teacher" – a shift of authority from the person to the text.

313.label: The Kaliver Rebbe (Rabbi Menachem Mendel Taub)
313.bio: A Holocaust survivor who turned the memory of the catastrophe into a mission of faith, Torah and spreading the recitation of "Shema Yisrael".
313.core_concept: Turning brokenness into a spiritual mission.

315.label: Rabbi Nachman Krochmal (Ranak)
315.bio: A thinker who made history a tool for understanding the eternity of Israel and for joining faith with modern criticism.

317.label: Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok
317.bio: A student of the Maharam of Rothenburg who documented his teacher's life in prison and turned living conduct into a halakhic source.
317.core_concept: Halakha out of life – documenting reality as a basis for ruling.

318.label: Rabbi Aharon HaKohen of Lunel
318.bio: Author of "Orchot Chaim" – a work combining halakha, ethics and mystery, preserving a crumbling Torah world.
318.core_concept: Halakha as a complete way of life – body, soul and mystery.

319.label: Rabbi Alexandri Zuslin HaKohen (the Maharach)
319.bio: Author of "Sefer HaAgudah" – a systematic summary of the Talmud meant to stabilise halakha after crises.
319.core_concept: Condensing and deciding – a move from pilpul to clear halakha.

320.label: Major Roi Klein
320.bio: An IDF officer who gave his life to save his soldiers and became a symbol of heroism that flows from a life of values.
320.core_concept: Heroism as the continuity of a life – not a single moment.

421.label: Rabbi Shlomo HaKohen of Vilna
421.bio: One of the great rabbis of Vilna, a central editor of the Vilna Talmud and an enthusiastic supporter of Hibbat Zion.
421.core_concept: Loyalty to tradition alongside recognising processes of redemption in history.

323.label: Rabbi Baruch Shapira
323.bio: A modern kabbalist who chose a life of seclusion in the desert, combining Lithuanian scholarship, Novardok mussar and practical, prophetic Kabbalah. He sought to revive the wisdom of letter combinations as a living path of attainment, not only a theoretical one.
323.core_concept: Kabbalah as a demanding way of life: refining the person until he becomes a vessel of attainment, joining Torah, science and consciousness in an accelerated modern age.

324.label: Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel (the Alter of Slabodka)
324.bio: Founder of the Slabodka school and shaper of the idea of "the greatness of man". He raised a central generation of leaders in the yeshiva world.
324.core_concept: The greatness of man as a basis for the service of God and for education.

326.label: Shlomo Molcho
326.bio: A daring kabbalist and messianic figure who went from Portuguese converso to a central figure in the redemption movements of the 16th century.
326.core_concept: Joining messianic vision with historical action.

327.label: Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz
327.bio: One of the great kabbalists of Safed and author of the poem "Lecha Dodi", which shaped the experience of welcoming the Sabbath for generations.
327.core_concept: Turning Kabbalah into a liturgical, experiential language.

328.label: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller
328.bio: The great commentator on the Mishnah and a leader of communities in a time of crisis and persecution in Europe.
328.core_concept: Renewing the study of the Mishnah as a basis for understanding the Talmud.

337.label: Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv (the Leshem)
337.bio: One of the great Lithuanian kabbalists of the modern era, author of an orderly system for understanding Kabbalah according to the Ari and the Vilna Gaon.
337.core_concept: Conceptual precision and intellectual responsibility in the study of Kabbalah.

339.label: Rabbi Yosef ben Yehuda ibn Shimon
339.bio: The Rambam's outstanding student and the addressee of the Guide of the Perplexed. A physician, philosopher and community leader.
339.core_concept: Intellectual perplexity as a lever for spiritual growth.

348.label: Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan
348.bio: Head of a yeshiva and shaper of the world of midrash in Europe, whose traditions deeply influenced Rashi's commentary.
348.core_concept: Preserving and passing on ancient midrashic traditions.

388.label: The Ralbag (Gersonides)
388.bio: A philosopher, commentator, mathematician and astronomer, one of the original thinkers of medieval Judaism.
388.core_concept: Human reason is a central tool for reaching the truth.

391.label: Rav Maimon the Dayyan
391.bio: The Rambam's father, a judge and community leader who shaped his son's spiritual and intellectual path.
391.core_concept: Combining Torah, science and human sensitivity.

397.label: Rabbi Yechiel ben Yekutiel Anav
397.bio: An Italian sage and physician who saved the complete text of the Yerushalmi and wrote one of the important books of ethics of the Middle Ages.
397.core_concept: Improving character traits as part of repairing the whole person.

416.label: Rabbi Kalman Shem Tov Gefen
416.bio: A thinker who tried to create a synthesis of Kabbalah, modern science and philosophy.
416.core_concept: Science and the Torah describe different layers of the same reality.

422.label: Rabbi Yisrael Yehoshua Trunk of Kutno
422.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of Poland and a central supporter of settling the Land and of the sale permit at the start of the settlement.
422.core_concept: National responsibility is part of the world of halakha.

425.label: Rabbi Meir ben Baruch HaLevi (Maharam Segal)
425.bio: One of the leaders of Ashkenazi Jewry after the great crises, and one of the shapers of the Ashkenazi institution of ordination.
425.core_concept: Building Torah authority out of communal responsibility.

426.label: Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer (Baruch She'amar)
426.bio: One of the great sages of sacred scribal art, who shaped the tradition of the form of the letters and crowns in writing holy books.
426.core_concept: Precision in the tradition of the script is part of the holiness of the Torah.

427.label: Rabbi Israel of Krems
427.bio: A halakhic authority and leader who preserved the tradition of Ashkenaz through his glosses on the rulings of the Rosh.
427.core_concept: Custom is a central source of authority in shaping halakha.

428.label: Rabbi David Gans
428.bio: A Jewish historian and astronomer who joined the world of Torah to the scientific revolution of the Renaissance.
428.core_concept: Science can serve as a tool for understanding creation.

429.label: Rabbi Moshe Zacuto (the Ramaz)
429.bio: A kabbalist, halakhic authority and Hebrew playwright who spread the Kabbalah of the Ari in Europe.
429.core_concept: Joining the world of mystery with practical life.

430.label: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai
430.bio: One of the central Tannaim who shaped the Oral Torah after the Bar Kokhba revolt.
430.core_concept: Building a stable society out of halakhic and moral responsibility.

431.label: Rabbi Meir Baal HaNes
431.bio: One of the great Tannaim, a central shaper of the Mishnah and a symbol of faith and salvation.
431.core_concept: Look at the inner essence and not only at the outside.

432.label: Rabbi Abraham Cohen de Herrera
432.bio: A kabbalist and thinker who built a bridge between the Kabbalah of the Ari and European philosophy.
432.core_concept: Mystery and reason complement each other in the search for truth.

434.label: The Rashbatz (Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemach Duran)
434.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of North Africa and its spiritual leader after the decrees of 1391.
434.core_concept: Rebuilding out of crisis, and joining Torah with general wisdom.

435.label: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
435.bio: A student of Rabbi Akiva and one of the greatest Tannaim, identified with the revelation of the teaching of mystery.
435.core_concept: Illuminating the world by joining inwardness and deed.

436.label: Rabbi Shalom Buzaglo
436.bio: A kabbalist and judge, author of the central systematic commentary on the Zohar.
436.core_concept: Making the world of mystery accessible through order, system and clarity.

437.label: Rav Yosef bar Chiya
437.bio: One of the great Amoraim of Babylonia and head of the Pumbedita yeshiva, known for his vast learning and for preserving the Talmudic tradition.
437.core_concept: Without a precise tradition there can be no true innovation.

438.label: Rav Yosef bar Chama
438.bio: A wealthy and influential sage from Mechoza, father of Rava and one of the shapers of the Torah elite of Babylonia.
438.core_concept: Combining Torah, public responsibility and an understanding of economic reality.

439.label: The Rama of Fano (Rabbi Menachem Azariah)
439.bio: One of the great kabbalists of Italy and a bridge between the Kabbalah of the Ramak and the Kabbalah of the Ari.
439.core_concept: Reason, halakha and the inner Torah can be joined together.

440.label: The Rashbash (Rabbi Shlomo ben Shimon Duran)
440.bio: One of the great sages of North Africa, who continued the Rashbatz's way in leading the Jewry of the Maghreb.
440.core_concept: Loyalty to tradition alongside responsibility for a changing reality.

441.label: Mahari Corcos
441.bio: A central commentator on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah and one of the builders of the halakhic foundation for the revival of the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel.
441.core_concept: Studying the Torah in its entirety is a preparation for redemption.

442.label: Rabbi Betzalel Ashkenazi
442.bio: Author of the "Shitah Mekubetzet" and a central rescuer of the literature of the Rishonim by collecting and editing rare manuscripts.
442.core_concept: Preserving Torah memory is building a world.

445.label: Rabbi Avraham Klausner
445.bio: One of the great sages of Austria and a central shaper of the tradition and customs of Ashkenaz after the crises of the 14th century.
445.core_concept: Custom preserves the soul of the community.

446.label: Rabbi Aharon Blumlein
446.bio: One of the leaders of Austrian Jewry, murdered in the Vienna persecutions, who preserved the tradition of Ashkenaz for generations.
446.core_concept: Preserving tradition is an act of spiritual heroism.

447.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Isaac Tyrnau
447.bio: Author of the book of customs that became one of the central foundations of the Ashkenazi way of life.
447.core_concept: Communal memory is the basis of Jewish continuity.

448.label: Sarah Our Matriarch
448.bio: Mother of the Israelite nation, a prophetess and the shaper of the spiritual identity of the house of Abraham.
448.core_concept: Holiness is built within the home, the family and life.

450.label: The Mahari Weil
450.bio: One of the great sages of Ashkenaz and a student of the Maharil, one of the shapers of Ashkenazi halakha after the crises of the Middle Ages.
450.core_concept: Halakhic ruling should rest on plain sense, clarity and responsibility.

451.label: Rabbi Yonah of Regensburg
451.bio: A student of Rabbi Yehuda HeChasid and a continuer of the tradition of the Ashkenazi Pietists, who combined moral leadership with communal ruling.
451.core_concept: Fear of Heaven is also tested in how one treats others and in social responsibility.

453.label: Rabbi Yaakov Margolioth of Nuremberg
453.bio: A halakhic authority and public leader, one of the shapers of the laws of divorce and chalitzah in late Ashkenaz.
453.core_concept: Traditional stability and halakhic caution in times of change.

454.label: The Maharam Mintz
454.bio: One of the great sages of Ashkenaz, who preserved the traditions of Mainz and passed them on to later generations.
454.core_concept: Keeping communal and halakhic continuity even in times of crisis.

455.label: Ruth the Moabite
455.bio: Mother of the royal house of David and a symbol of kindness, loyalty and accepting the Torah by choice.
455.core_concept: Kindness and loyalty can change the course of history.

456.label: Rabbi Dr. Avraham Livni
456.bio: A thinker and convert who saw the return to Zion as a spiritual answer to the crisis of Western culture.
456.core_concept: The State of Israel is a spiritual process of universal meaning.

460.label: Rabbenu David Bonafed
460.bio: A student of the Ramban and one of the deepest scholars of the Catalan beit midrash.
460.core_concept: Understanding the inner structure of the Talmudic sugya.

461.label: The Maharam of Padua
461.bio: A central halakhic authority in Italy who stood at the crossroads between the tradition of Ashkenaz and the printing revolution.
461.core_concept: Combining loyalty to tradition with human sensitivity.

462.label: The Holy Ari
462.bio: The renewer of Lurianic Kabbalah and a central shaper of the concepts of contraction, breaking and repair.
462.core_concept: Man is an active partner in the repair of creation.

465.label: Rabbi Yosef ibn Tabul
465.bio: A student of the Ari who preserved and spread an independent tradition of Lurianic Kabbalah.
465.core_concept: Many traditions can reveal different faces of the same truth.

466.label: Rabbi Yaakov ben Chananel Sikili
466.bio: A student of the Rashba who stressed the holiness of the Land and the renewal of national life in the Land of Israel.
466.core_concept: Redemption also requires human initiative and action.

468.label: Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin
468.bio: A rabbi, writer and editor of the Talmudic Encyclopedia, who joined scholarship, Hasidism and modern writing.
468.core_concept: Order and clarity can be created without losing the depth of the Torah.

470.label: The Aderet (Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim)
470.bio: Rabbi of Ponevezh, Mir and Jerusalem, and father-in-law of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook.
470.core_concept: Greatness in Torah demands public responsibility and personal example.

471.label: Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla
471.bio: One of the great kabbalists of Spain, who ordered the system of the sefirot and the holy names.
471.core_concept: Nature and holiness are different revelations of the same divine reality.

472.label: Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank
472.bio: Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem and one of the great halakhic authorities of the Land of Israel in the period of revival and the founding of the State.
472.core_concept: Halakhic ruling should combine loyalty to tradition with national responsibility.

477.label: Rabbi Solomon ibn Gabirol
477.bio: A poet and philosopher, one of the greats of the Golden Age of Spain. He wrote "Keter Malkhut" and "Mekor Chaim" – a philosophical work that also influenced Christian thought in the Middle Ages.
477.core_concept: Combining sacred poetry with Neoplatonic philosophy – the soul ascends to the source of life through contemplation and knowledge.

479.label: Maharash of Neustadt (Rabbi Shalom of Neustadt)
479.bio: One of the great sages of Ashkenaz in the generation before the Maharil, and his principal teacher. His teaching and customs were recorded in "Halachot uMinhagei Maharash" and shaped the tradition of Ashkenazi custom.
479.core_concept: Custom as a binding halakhic source – documenting the customs of the communities as a basis for ruling.

480.label: Rabbi Reuven Margaliot
480.bio: A Torah scholar and remarkable bibliographer, winner of the Israel Prize for Torah literature. He wrote dozens of books on the study of the Talmud, the Zohar and halakha, and directed the Rambam Library in Tel Aviv.
480.core_concept: Bibliographic precision as a Torah tool – locating and cross-checking sources reveals the continuity of tradition.

481.label: Rabbi Yehuda Moscato
481.bio: One of the great preachers of Italian Jewry in the Renaissance. He wrote the collection of sermons "Nefutzot Yehuda" and "Kol Yehuda" – the classic commentary on the Kuzari.
481.core_concept: Merging Renaissance learning with the tradition of Israel – rhetoric, music and philosophy in the service of the sermon.

482.label: Shmuel (the Amora)
482.bio: One of the great Amoraim of Babylonia and head of the Nehardea yeshiva, who established the independence of the Babylonian Torah centre from the Land of Israel. He combined halakhic greatness with expertise in astronomy and medicine, and laid down the principle "the law of the kingdom is the law", which regulated life in the Diaspora.
482.core_concept: Realistic leadership – a halakhic anchor for Jewish existence in the Diaspora through "the law of the kingdom is the law" and mastery of the world's sciences.

483.label: Shimon Bar Kokhba
483.bio: Leader of the last revolt against Rome (132–136), who established a short-lived Jewish sovereignty in Judea with an administration, coins and systems of hideouts. The Sages were divided over him – between messianism and disappointment – and in modern times he returned as a symbol of national heroism.
483.core_concept: Sovereignty as a religious-national value – the last organised attempt at earthly redemption by human force.

484.label: Rabbi Yisrael Najara
484.bio: One of the great poets after the Expulsion from Spain, author of "Yah Ribon Alam". He combined melodies from the Ottoman world with intense religious passion, and at the end of his life served as rabbi of Gaza. His poetry made the piyyut a medium of accessible holiness.
484.core_concept: Holiness enters through melody – "converting" foreign tunes and turning song into an emotional, intimate service of God.

485.label: Theodos of Rome
485.bio: Leader of the Rome community in the period of the Tannaim. He instituted eating a "roasted kid" on Passover nights, stirring a controversy with the Sages, and was known for his homily on the self-sacrifice of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah as a model for Diaspora Jewry.
485.core_concept: Jewish leadership in the Diaspora – preserving identity and sanctifying God's name far from the centre in the Land of Israel.

486.label: Rabbenu Yonah Gerondi
486.bio: One of the great Rishonim of Spain, author of "Sha'arei Teshuvah" and "Aliyot deRabbenu Yonah". He turned repentance from the piety of a select few into a religious duty for all Israel, and joined the study traditions of France and Spain.
486.core_concept: The democratisation of ethics – repentance as a way of life binding on every person.

487.label: Chacham David Nieto
487.bio: Rabbi of the Spanish and Portuguese community in London at the start of the 18th century, a physician and astronomer. In his book "Mateh Dan" he defended the authority of the Oral Torah with rational tools, and fought deism and Sabbateanism.
487.core_concept: Nature is providence – identifying the laws of nature as direct divine action, as a rational answer to deism.

488.label: Rabbi Shlomo Ephraim of Luntschitz (the Kli Yakar)
488.bio: Author of the commentary "Kli Yakar" on the Torah, a preacher and head of a yeshiva who served in the Prague rabbinate alongside the Maharal and as his successor. He combined plain-sense interpretation with sharp moral and social criticism of the pursuit of money, corrupt leadership and detached scholarship.
488.core_concept: Interpretation as rebuke – the plain sense of Scripture as a tool for improving character and society.

489.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Yaakov Reines
489.bio: Founder of the Mizrachi movement and of the Lida yeshiva, which combined sacred and secular studies. He developed a logical, conceptual method of Gemara study, and led a pragmatic political Zionism that put saving the people's lives before considerations of miraculous redemption.
489.core_concept: Separating the needs of the hour from redemption – a halakhic and ideological foundation for practical political Zionism.

490.label: Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Zuckerman
490.bio: One of the outstanding students of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook and a key figure in religious Zionism. He founded educational institutions and social movements such as "El Ami", advocated manual labour and refused to make a living from the Torah, and made the teaching of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook accessible to his generation.
490.core_concept: Judaism as "the nature of life" – faith built out of pioneering action, labour and educational work.

491.label: Rabbi Shlomo Goren
491.bio: The first Chief Military Rabbi and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel. He created a halakhic foundation for the army and Israeli sovereignty, released the agunot of fallen IDF soldiers, and formed an orderly teaching on national questions – from the laws of war to ascending the Temple Mount.
491.core_concept: State halakha – adapting halakha to the state and a modern army out of the sanctity of human life and courage in ruling.

492.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner
492.bio: Head of the Rabbenu Chaim Berlin yeshiva in New York and author of the "Pachad Yitzchak" series. He merged analytic Lithuanian scholarship with Hasidic and moral depth, and developed an educational teaching that sees a person's crises as a necessary ground for spiritual growth.
492.core_concept: "The greatness of man" – the fall and the crisis as necessary stages in building the spiritual personality.

493.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Eizik Chaver
493.bio: One of the great sages of 19th-century Lithuania and a continuer of the Vilna Gaon's tradition in Kabbalah. He wrote the responsa "Binyan Olam" and "Magen VeTzinah" in defence of the antiquity of the Zohar against the maskilim's criticism, and interpreted Kabbalah in a theoretical way that rejects all corporeality.
493.core_concept: Systematic Lithuanian Kabbalah – making the Vilna Gaon's hidden teaching accessible as an ordered theoretical system against the challenges of modernity.

494.label: Rabbenu Simcha of Vitry
494.bio: One of Rashi's outstanding students and the editor of "Machzor Vitry" – a comprehensive compendium of halakha, prayer and custom that preserved the teaching of Rashi's school and decisively shaped the Ashkenazi rite and patterns of ruling in Europe.
494.core_concept: Preservation as revolution – fixing oral traditions into a written code that shaped Ashkenazi prayer for generations.

495.label: Rabbi Moshe de León
495.bio: One of the great kabbalists of 13th-century Castile, through whom the Zohar was revealed (or edited). He also wrote kabbalistic books in Hebrew such as "Shekel HaKodesh", and stood at the centre of the historical controversy over the antiquity of the Zohar.
495.core_concept: Placing the Zohar at the centre of the Jewish bookshelf – the founding text of the teaching of mystery.

496.label: Prof. Nechama Leibowitz
496.bio: The teacher of the generation in Bible study. Her weekly "Gilyonot" (1942–1993) taught generations to read biblical commentary with critical attention, and made the study of the weekly portion the possession of all.
496.core_concept: The democratisation of biblical interpretation – every learner can and must compare commentators and ask "What troubles Rashi?".

497.label: Rabbi Eliyahu Eliezer Dessler
497.bio: One of the great figures of the Mussar movement in the 20th century, a product of the Kelm yeshiva and spiritual supervisor of the Ponevezh yeshiva. In his book "Michtav MeEliyahu" he formed a deep understanding of the human soul, free will and giving.
497.core_concept: "The point of choice" – the real struggle between good and evil takes place on the shifting border between habit and the absence of choice; and the idea that a person loves the one to whom he gives, not only the one who gives to him.

498.label: Rabbi Yehuda Coriat
498.bio: One of the prominent kabbalists of Moroccan Jewry and later one of the sages of Livorno. He wrote "Ma'or VaShemesh" (1839), a treasury of kabbalistic traditions of Spain and the Maghreb, and was the teacher and uncle of Rabbi Eliyahu Benamozegh.
498.core_concept: Preservation and transmission – gathering ancient kabbalistic traditions from Morocco and Spain under one roof, which gave a basis for the growth of the original thought of his student Benamozegh.

499.label: Rabbi Haviv Toledano
499.bio: A sage of Meknes who sought to strengthen the foundations of faith against new European influences. He wrote "Terumat HaKodesh" and compiled a detailed family tree of the Toledano family.
499.core_concept: Keeping tradition as a blend of Torah education and passing on historical and family memory; in later generations his descendants continued on a path of outreach and explanation rather than withdrawal.

501.label: The Tzemach Tzedek (Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn)
501.bio: The third Rebbe of Chabad, who combined Hasidic leadership with wide-ranging halakhic ruling in the responsa "Tzemach Tzedek", and worked to free agunot and to defend Russian Jewry against the decrees of the Tsarist regime.
501.core_concept: Joining Hasidism and halakha – independence of thought in ruling with loyalty to tradition, alongside firm public resistance to political pressure (the St Petersburg conference, the affair of the cantonists).

502.label: Rabbi Dovber Schneuri (the Mitteler Rebbe)
502.bio: The second Rebbe of Chabad, who moved the centre of the movement to Lubavitch, systematically expanded his father's ideas ("Rechovot HaNahar"), and worked to found agricultural colonies and strengthen the Jewish community in Hebron.
502.core_concept: A systematic expansion of Hasidic thought alongside practical social and economic responsibility – institutionalising Hasidism as a movement with institutions and wide public activity, not only around the founder's figure.

503.label: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah
503.bio: A student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and one of the great sages of the Yavne generation. He earned his living as a smith, decided the dispute over "the oven of Akhnai" with the principle "it is not in heaven", and represented the Jewish public before the Roman authorities.
503.core_concept: "It is not in heaven" – after the giving of the Torah, halakhic decision rests with the judgement of the Sages and not with signs and wonders from heaven.

506.label: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah
506.bio: A descendant of Ezra the Scribe, he was appointed head of the Sanhedrin at eighteen following the leadership crisis around Rabban Gamliel. He removed the restriction on entering the beit midrash and greatly widened the circle of learners.
506.core_concept: Opening the gates of the beit midrash to all who seek to learn – the spiritual power of the Torah grows precisely as the number of learners widens.

507.label: Rabbi Eliezer the Great (Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus)
507.bio: A student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and founder of the Lod yeshiva, known for his absolute loyalty to tradition. In the dispute over "the oven of Akhnai" signs from heaven were brought in support of his view, but it was rejected on principle and he was eventually excommunicated.
507.core_concept: Absolute loyalty to the tradition handed down from Sinai, even when it leads to confrontation with the majority and a heavy personal price – excommunication and loneliness until the day of his death.

508.label: Rabbi Eliyahu ben Chaim (the Ra'anach)
508.bio: He served as Chacham Bashi of Constantinople and united communities of different traditions in the Ottoman Empire under his authority. His testimony in his responsa on the acceptance of Rabbi Yosef Karo's rulings is a central historical source, and he checked the biblical text against the Aleppo Codex.
508.core_concept: The halakhic unification of divided communities under an agreed ruling authority, and precise historical documentation of the acceptance of the Shulchan Arukh as the central code.

509.label: Rabbi Chaim ben Attar (the Or HaChaim)
509.bio: One of the great sages of Morocco in the 18th century, a commentator, halakhic authority and kabbalist. He wrote the "Or HaChaim", which combines plain sense, allusion, homily and mystery, and founded the Knesset Yisrael yeshiva in Jerusalem. The Baal Shem Tov mourned him on his death: "The western candle has gone out."
509.core_concept: A systematic combination of the four levels of interpretation (PaRDeS) in one commentary, alongside a conception of redemption that distinguishes between a swift "I will hasten it" and a gradual "in its time".

510.label: Sarah Schenirer
510.bio: Founder of the Beit Yaakov network, who in 1918 opened a first class of seven pupils that within less than two decades grew into hundreds of schools and tens of thousands of pupils. She won the support of the Chofetz Chaim and the leaders of Agudat Yisrael.
510.core_concept: Building a system of systematic Torah education for girls in the face of gaps in general education, combining scholarship with emotional and experiential depth.

511.label: Rebbetzin Vichna Kaplan
511.bio: Sarah Schenirer's outstanding student, she founded the Beit Yaakov network in the United States in 1937, from a small class in her home in Williamsburg to a large educational institution with a dormitory, high school and teachers' seminary.
511.core_concept: Adapting the European Beit Yaakov model to American reality, combining high spiritual demands with personal attention and educational sensitivity.

512.label: Rebbetzin Dr. Bruria David
512.bio: The daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner, with a doctorate from Columbia University, she founded and directed the Sarah Schenirer Institute in Jerusalem as an elite institution of Haredi women's scholarship, and headed the editing of her father's books after his death.
512.core_concept: Raising women's scholarship to a high intellectual level without challenging the boundaries of the traditional structure of the Torah world.

513.label: Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg
513.bio: One of the founders of the world of teshuvah for women, she established the EYAHT midrasha in 1984, which grew into an international study centre for women. Alongside her husband, Rabbi Noah Weinberg, she combined deep scholarship, work on character and raising a large family.
513.core_concept: "It is not enough to be good – we must be great" – deep, demanding study for women as a way of fulfilling a personal calling, not a renunciation out of false humility.

514.label: Rebbetzin Esther Jungreis
514.bio: A Holocaust survivor who founded the Hineni movement in 1973, which grew into a network of educational institutions, heritage centres and social projects. She warned against the "spiritual holocaust" of assimilation and disconnection from tradition.
514.core_concept: Responding to the destruction of the Holocaust by building a new Jewish generation connected to the Torah, not only by remembering the grief – responsibility instead of despair.

515.label: Rebbetzin Bracha Qafih
515.bio: A woman of kindness and community leader, she founded the "Segulat Naomi" association, which helped thousands of families in Jerusalem. Her husband, Rabbi Yosef Qafih, devoted himself to editing the Rambam's writings, while she built the economic and social foundation for the family and the community.
515.core_concept: Kindness as an organised and dignified system rather than a one-off act – combining a big heart with careful order and management in order to preserve the dignity of those who receive.

516.label: Rebbetzin Sarah Herzog
516.bio: The wife of Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Isaac Herzog, she led a broad social enterprise: founding the Emunah movement in 1959, developing the Herzog Hospital, and encouraging education and employment for religious women.
516.core_concept: Combining halakhic loyalty with active public involvement – a woman contributes to building society and the nation, not only the home.

517.label: Tova Sanhedrai-Goldreich
517.bio: The first religious woman member of the Knesset, one of the leaders of the Emunah movement and founder of the "List of the Religious Working Woman" in 1949. She served four terms in the Knesset for the National Religious Party and advanced social and welfare legislation.
517.core_concept: Combining halakhic commitment with public and parliamentary responsibility – widening religious women's participation in building the State without giving up principles.

518.label: Rabbi Amos Kamus Chaim Guetta
518.bio: A kabbalist and head of a yeshiva, leader of the Libyan Jewish community in Netanya, who founded the yeshiva and beit midrash "Rabbi Yitzchak Chai Taieb". He lived very simply and refused to accept personal payment, and was murdered in his home and beit midrash on 17 Tammuz 5786 (2026).
518.core_concept: Combining kabbalistic depth with extreme personal simplicity and humility – spiritual leadership open and available to every person, without barriers.

519.label: Sarah Stern-Katan
519.bio: A survivor of the Łódź ghetto and Auschwitz, a social worker and member of the Knesset for the National Religious Party, she served as president of the Emunah movement. She joined the values of "Torah and labour" with professional training in social work.
519.core_concept: Acts of kindness as a professional system and not only good will – strengthening social welfare as a practical expression of the Torah's commandments and of human dignity.

520.label: Henrietta Szold
520.bio: An educator and Zionist, founder of the Hadassah organisation and leader of Youth Aliyah. She studied Talmud at JTS on condition that she would not be ordained as a rabbi, and wrote the "Kaddish letter" on women's spiritual commitment.
520.core_concept: Combining tradition, Zionism and kindness – rescuing children in Youth Aliyah included preserving their spiritual and cultural world alongside physical rescue.

522.label: Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel
522.bio: One of the great Amoraim of Babylonia, a student of Rav and Shmuel, who after the destruction of Nehardea founded the Pumbedita yeshiva, which lasted almost eight hundred years. He joined the traditions of Sura and Nehardea into a new school and influenced the customs of blessings and prayer.
522.core_concept: "Whoever wishes to be pious should fulfil the laws of damages" – true piety is measured by honesty and care not to harm others, not only by asceticism.

523.label: Bathsheba
523.bio: The wife of David and mother of Solomon, who in the Book of Kings emerges as a determined political figure: she acts with Nathan the prophet to secure Solomon's coronation and then gains the status of "queen mother". In rabbinic tradition she is identified with the mother of Lemuel, who rebukes her son about the responsibility of kingship.
523.core_concept: The crown is not only a right but a moral responsibility; Bathsheba represents the power to set limits to the king and to demand of him justice, self-discipline and care for the weak.

524.label: Doña Gracia Nasi
524.bio: An influential 16th-century Jewish leader, born into a converso family, who turned her wealth, trading networks and political connections into a rescue enterprise for persecuted Jews. She supported the printing of books and Torah scholars, led the attempted boycott of Ancona and was a partner in the vision of establishing a Jewish centre in Tiberias.
524.core_concept: Economic and political power is a public responsibility: wealth, connections and influence can be turned into a tool of rescue, cultural rebuilding and building a Jewish future in the Land of Israel.

525.label: Rabbi Aryeh Kaplan
525.bio: A rabbi, physicist, translator and scholar of Kabbalah who worked in the United States and made Judaism accessible to a modern public. He dealt with the relationship between Torah and science, the age of the universe and the reconstruction of Jewish meditative traditions from kabbalistic and Hasidic books, and wrote "The Living Torah".
525.core_concept: A modern Jew need not choose between intellect and faith; scientific and psychological language can be used to go deeper into the sources and to translate an ancient tradition into a contemporary world of concepts.

526.label: Rabbi Dr. Azriel Hildesheimer
526.bio: A rabbi, scholar and educator who worked in Germany and Hungary and founded the Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin. He combined deep Torah study with academic training and modern research tools, and also worked to strengthen the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel and its economic independence.
526.core_concept: The modern world and research do not require giving up tradition; the tools of the academy can be used from a Torah starting point to build a Jewish leadership able to meet the challenges of the time.

527.label: Rabbi Yehuda Leib Don Yahia
527.bio: A rabbi, scholar and thinker who combined in his world Brisker scholarship, Hasidic tradition and the vision of religious Zionism. He was a student of Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik, took part in founding the Mizrachi movement, and saw settling the Land and building national institutions as a practical expression of faith.
527.core_concept: Faith is not passive waiting but a force that demands action: just as a person builds a sukkah to make room for holiness, so building the Land and national revival can be a religious act that brings the people's powers from potential into actuality.

528.label: Rabbi Yaakov Zvi Mecklenburg
528.bio: Rabbi of Königsberg and author of "HaKetav VeHaKabbalah", who sought to show through grammar, linguistics and philology the inner link between the Written Torah and the tradition of the Sages. He fought Reform but used modern research tools, and even supported natural studies and the settlement of the Land of Israel.
528.core_concept: Modern intellectual tools can be used precisely to deepen and defend tradition; openness to method does not require giving up commitment to the Torah.

529.label: Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel
529.bio: A rabbi, preacher, printer and thinker from a Portuguese converso family, who founded a Hebrew printing house in Amsterdam and wrote for Jews and Christian scholars alike. He negotiated with Oliver Cromwell for the readmission of the Jews to England, out of a messianic view of history.
529.core_concept: Messianic faith does not require passive waiting; it can drive action in the real world through printing, thought, diplomacy and dialogue with cultures and governments.

530.label: Rabbi Mordechai Eliasberg
530.bio: Rabbi of Bauska, a halakhic authority and one of the first rabbis active in practice in the Hibbat Zion movement. He sought to join full loyalty to halakha with science, labour, agriculture and national building, and distinguished between the "body of the commandment" of building the Land and its Torah "soul".
530.core_concept: The material and spiritual building of the Land can go up together; national cooperation is possible even between parts of the people who differ in outlook, as long as a clear Torah identity is kept.

531.label: Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi (Rabbi Yehuda Margoza)
531.bio: The first rabbi of modern Jaffa, who united communities, absorbed immigrants and founded public institutions. In 1842 he planted the first Jewish orange grove of modern times, supported Mikveh Israel and encouraged labour, agriculture and settlement in the Land.
531.core_concept: Torah and working the land do not contradict each other; building the Land, economic independence and public initiative are part of the process of redemption.

532.label: Rebbetzin Batsheva Esther Kanievsky
532.bio: The daughter of Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, granddaughter of Rabbi Aryeh Levin and wife of Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky. Her home in Bnei Brak became an address for thousands of women seeking advice, prayer and encouragement, and a centre of charity, help for families and support for the sick.
532.core_concept: Spiritual influence does not depend on an official role: personal listening, kindness and simple faith can turn a private home into a centre of hope and love of Israel.

533.label: Hannah Szenes
533.bio: A poet, paratrooper and hero of the Yishuv who came from Hungary to the Land of Israel and joined a parachute mission behind enemy lines in Europe. In her diaries and poems she joined Jewish identity, prayer, moral responsibility and national mission.
533.core_concept: True spirituality does not shut itself off from reality but demands action; prayer, responsibility for the people and readiness to act can merge into one moral mission.

534.label: Yalta
534.bio: The daughter of the family of the Exilarch and wife of Rav Nachman, one of the prominent women of the Talmud. She expresses original halakhic ideas, holds her ground against sages, seeks a further halakhic ruling when needed and even advises her husband on matters of leadership.
534.core_concept: The world of halakha includes not only prohibitions but also a space of permission, pleasure and holiness; Yalta embodies intellectual independence, public standing and an active female presence in the world of the Amoraim.

535.label: Zeruiah
535.bio: The sister of King David and daughter of Jesse, whose name is preserved in Scripture mainly through her three sons – Joab, Abishai and Asahel. The repeated naming of the sons after their mother made Zeruiah a family symbol identified with strength, heroism and loyalty to the house of David.
535.core_concept: The tension between David and the sons of Zeruiah shows the need and the danger in joining kindness and force: kingship needs military strength, but also moral restraint and spiritual leadership.

536.label: Rav Chisda
536.bio: One of the great Amoraim of Babylonia in the second and third generations, a student of Rav and head of the Sura yeshiva in his last years. He rose from poverty to wealth through his business, supported Torah and the needy, and was known for his scholarly sharpness and rulings sensitive to fairness and the protection of the weak.
536.core_concept: Combining Torah with economic independence and social responsibility: wealth, scholarship and leadership gain value when they serve honesty, kindness and the building of Torah institutions.

537.label: Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea
537.bio: A rabbi, judge and kabbalist from Mantua who combined deep engagement with Kabbalah with mathematics, geometry and astronomy. He wrote "Emunat Chachamim" in defence of Kabbalah and the Zohar, dealt with calendar calculations and Euclid, and supported the Ramchal when he aroused suspicion among the sages of Europe.
537.core_concept: Tradition can be defended by using reason, science and criticism; scientific knowledge need not undermine faith but can exist alongside it within a complete Torah world.

538.label: Rabbi Avraham ben Yitzchak min HaHar
538.bio: A sage of Provence whose commentaries on the Talmud were rediscovered after some of them had been attributed to other sages for generations. He combined careful study of the sugya, clarification of textual variants and halakhic decision, and also used the Rambam's writings in Arabic and outside knowledge in his study.
538.core_concept: The discovery of manuscripts can change the picture of Torah history; true study requires clarifying sources, variants and reality alongside clear ruling.

539.label: The Vilna Gaon (Rabbi Eliyahu ben Shlomo Zalman)
539.bio: One of the great sages of Israel in the modern era, who devoted himself to study and refused public office. He called for a return to the plain sense of the sugya and to the sources of the Sages, combined the revealed Torah, Kabbalah and the natural sciences, and influenced the yeshiva world and the immigration of his students to the Land of Israel.
539.core_concept: Precision in the sources and joining fields of knowledge are the key to understanding the Torah; personal seclusion can give rise to a broad educational and historical revolution.

540.label: Rabbi Baruch Schick of Shklov
540.bio: A Lithuanian rabbi, judge and physician who worked to make mathematics, astronomy and medicine accessible in Hebrew. He translated and adapted Euclid's Elements, wrote scientific books, and testified that the Vilna Gaon encouraged him to spread the sciences needed to understand the Torah.
540.core_concept: Knowledge of the sciences does not necessarily stand against the Torah; it can complete its understanding, help with halakhic questions and strengthen the intellectual dignity of Israel.

541.label: Rabbi Gedalia Nadel
541.bio: One of the close students of the Chazon Ish and a halakhic authority in the Chazon Ish neighbourhood, known for his independent way of study and his drive to understand the idea behind each commandment. Alongside his halakhic and public zeal, he held that there is no necessary contradiction between the theory of evolution and the Torah, and saw science as a tool for clarifying the truth.
541.core_concept: Faith need not fear the truth; deep loyalty to the Torah can be combined with intellectual honesty, the study of nature and understanding the spiritual and moral principle behind halakha.

542.label: Rabbi Chaim Vital
542.bio: The Ari's central student, who edited and wrote down the essentials of his teaching and so ensured its preservation for generations. Alongside Kabbalah he dealt with astronomy, medicine and alchemy, and saw the study of nature as part of understanding the divine order.
542.core_concept: The spiritual world and the physical world work in one order whose source is the Creator; studying creation and studying mystery can complement each other.

543.label: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
543.bio: An Amora of the Land of Israel of the third generation and a student of Rabbi Yochanan, known for halakha, aggadah and piety. The Sages tell that he asked the Angel of Death for thirty more days to review his learning, and that he sought to live so that his Torah would be tested against his deeds.
543.core_concept: The Torah is not only knowledge but a whole way of life: blessing, charity, struggling with the inclination and responsibility towards creation turn study into life itself.

544.label: Rabbi Yosef Shlomo Delmedigo (the Yashar of Candia)
544.bio: A rabbi, physician, mathematician and astronomer who studied with Galileo at the University of Padua. He accepted the heliocentric model and combined scientific knowledge with Torah study, while engaging in a complex way with Kabbalah and the Zohar.
544.core_concept: New scientific knowledge need not threaten tradition; it can be used to deepen the understanding of creation, halakha and the wisdom of the Torah.

545.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Chizkiya Lampronti
545.bio: Rabbi of Ferrara, head of a yeshiva and qualified physician, author of the halakhic encyclopedia "Pachad Yitzchak". He collected thousands of sources and rulings, and brought scientific clarification of reality into halakhic discussion out of loyalty to tradition.
545.core_concept: Science does not replace the Torah but helps clarify the reality to which halakha applies; loyalty to the Sages can go together with re-examining natural facts.

546.label: Rabbi Israel Lipschitz
546.bio: Rabbi of Danzig and author of the commentary "Tiferet Yisrael" on the Mishnah. He combined halakhic conservatism and personal asceticism with broad openness to the natural sciences, medicine and the wisdom of the nations, and even tried to fit geological discoveries and fossils into a Torah picture of the world.
546.core_concept: Openness to science does not require giving up tradition; the findings of the modern world can be examined and fitted into a firm framework of faith and halakha.

547.label: Rabbi Meir the Great of Premishlan
547.bio: One of the close students of the Baal Shem Tov and one of the leaders of the first generation of Hasidism. He was a deep kabbalist and a fighter against the Frankists, yet chose in humility to teach small children and to see the letters of the alphabet as a gate to the secrets of the Torah.
547.core_concept: Spiritual greatness is tested in humility and in willingness to deal with the simple foundations; a child's letters can carry the same secrets found in the worlds of Kabbalah.

548.label: Rabbi Pinchas Eliyahu Horowitz (the Sefer HaBrit)
548.bio: Author of "Sefer HaBrit HaShalem", a broad work that combined astronomy, physics, medicine and technology with Kabbalah, the soul and ethics. He sought to present knowledge of nature as a preparation for knowing the spiritual world, and to set love of others at the centre of life.
548.core_concept: Studying science and knowing creation can be a gateway to the service of God, but knowledge is a means, not an end; the supreme test of wisdom is how a person does good to others.

549.label: Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch
549.bio: A rabbi, commentator and Jewish thinker from Germany who formulated the approach of "Torah im Derech Eretz". In Frankfurt he led an educational system that combined sacred and general studies, and fought Reform while stressing full commitment to halakha within modern culture.
549.core_concept: One can take part in modern science, culture and society without the Torah losing its centrality; openness to the world demands a clear Torah identity and firm halakhic boundaries.

550.label: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I
550.bio: Head of the Sanhedrin on the eve of the destruction of the Second Temple and one of the leaders of the moderate camp in Jerusalem. He tried to curb internal violence and protect the people's future, and his rulings showed sensitivity to economic hardship and public needs.
550.core_concept: "Not study but action is the main thing" – Torah leadership is tested by public responsibility, integrity and the ability to turn values into action in a reality of crisis.

551.label: Rami bar Papa
551.bio: An early Babylonian Amora who was active before the famous Rav Papa, and is mentioned in sugyot in Yoma and Menachot. His name became part of the list of "the ten sons of Rav Papa" recited at the completion of a tractate, although chronology suggests he was not the biological son of Rav Papa, head of the Naresh yeshiva.
