551.core_concept: His figure links creative halakhic discussion with the memorial tradition of the yeshiva world; his name became part of the completion ceremony of Talmud learners for generations.

552.label: Rafram bar Pappa
552.bio: A Babylonian Amora of the fourth generation, a student of Rav Chisda and a contemporary of Rava. He passed on teachings in the name of Rav Chisda, dealt with practical ruling on sha'atnez, bailees and fasting, and transmitted aggadic traditions about the effect of the Temple's destruction on the order of the world.
552.core_concept: Great halakha is born from the meeting of tradition and an understanding of reality; with Rafram, practical precision and cosmic thought about the Temple exist in the same Torah world.

553.label: Serach bat Asher
553.bio: The daughter of Asher, who in rabbinic tradition became the keeper of the memory of the generations: she tells Jacob that Joseph is alive, keeps the sign of redemption "I have surely remembered", helps Moses find Joseph's coffin, and is even identified with the wise woman of Abel Beth Maacah.
553.core_concept: Whoever keeps memory can recognise redemption and act for the peace of the people; Serach embodies continuity between distant generations and the passing on of a living tradition.

554.label: Oenomaus of Gadara
554.bio: A Cynic philosopher from Gadara whom the Sages saw as "the greatest of the philosophers of the nations". He was a conversation partner of the Sages and the author of a sharp polemic against belief in fate.
554.core_concept: Man is responsible for his deeds and is not bound by fate: Oenomaus attacked the belief in fate and the oracles in the name of free will, and in the literature of the Sages, if the identification holds, he is a gentile sage who respects the Torah and those who study it.

555.label: Abraham Our Father
555.bio: The father of the nation. He left Ur of the Chaldees at the call of "Go forth", spread faith in the One God and made the Covenant between the Pieces.
555.core_concept: Faith in the One God that becomes a way of life: setting out into the unknown at God's word, kindness open to every person, and an everlasting covenant between God and his descendants.

556.label: Bruriah
556.bio: The renowned learned woman of the Tannaitic generation, wife of Rabbi Meir and daughter of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon. Her rulings and scholarship are cited in the Talmud – "three hundred teachings in a day".
556.core_concept: Learning and moral wisdom that do not depend on rank: Bruriah ruled on the laws of purity, taught to pray for an end to sins rather than to sinners, and faced her tragedies with courage.

557.label: King David
557.bio: Founder of the royal house of David and author of the Book of Psalms. He conquered Jerusalem and brought the Ark of the Covenant up to it – "the sweet singer of Israel".
557.core_concept: Kingship in Israel rests on humility and repentance before God: David united the people around Jerusalem, and in the Psalms turned his struggles, his falls and his hope into a prayer for all generations.

558.label: The Baal Shem Tov (Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov)
558.bio: The founder of the Hasidic movement. He taught that no place is empty of God, set devotion, joy and love of every Jew at the centre of the service of God – and changed the face of Eastern European Jewry.
558.core_concept: No place is empty of Him – the service of God in devotion and joy.

560.label: Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki (the Zera Avraham)
560.bio: Rishon LeZion and author of the responsa "Zera Avraham". One of the leaders of Jerusalem in the struggle against Sabbateanism and in fortifying the city's Torah standing.
560.core_concept: Guarding the walls of tradition in a time of crisis: an uncompromising fight against Sabbateanism, alongside rulings that do not shrink from stringency or innovation when the hour demands it, as in keeping women from becoming agunot.

561.label: Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Yitzchaki (the Rav of Porat)
561.bio: A rabbi active in Israel who combines kabbalistic tradition with making the hidden teaching accessible digitally. He heads the "David HaMelech" beit midrash in Moshav Porat, a centre for studying the Zohar and for hitbodedut.
561.core_concept: Making Kabbalah accessible as a practical tool for repairing the soul in the digital age.

562.label: Rabbi Aharon Kotler
562.bio: Founder of the Lakewood yeshiva and the architect of the Torah world in America after the Holocaust. He set Torah study for its own sake as the supreme value, without compromise.
562.core_concept: Torah study for its own sake, whole and without compromise, is what will ensure the people's continuity after the Holocaust: a yeshiva of learners in the heart of America, not an adaptation of the Torah to the surrounding culture.

563.label: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (the Rayatz)
563.bio: The sixth Rebbe of Chabad. He stood firm against the Soviet regime, was released from a death sentence, and moved the centre of Chabad to America.
563.core_concept: Self-sacrifice as the driving force of leadership: keeping the Torah alive underground against Soviet repression, and declaring that 'America is no different': Judaism can flourish anywhere.

564.label: Rabbi Lord Jonathan Sacks
564.bio: Chief Rabbi of Britain and a Jewish thinker of worldwide influence. He presented the voice of the Torah in the language of philosophy and universal ethics.
564.core_concept: 'The dignity of difference': keeping one's religious distinctiveness is a key to peace, not an obstacle to it, and faith is a call to moral responsibility, to covenant and to repairing the world.

565.label: Rabbi Mordechai Atiya
565.bio: A kabbalist and head of the kabbalists' yeshiva, one of the sages of Aleppo who settled in Jerusalem. He called for redemption through the hidden teaching and action.
565.core_concept: Zionism does not contradict religion but is a stage in a Kabbalistic process of redemption: going up to the Land is a great commandment that may not be put off, and the study of the hidden Torah is a way of life that sanctifies every movement and every word of prayer.

566.label: Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel
566.bio: Spiritual supervisor of the Sha'alvim yeshiva and a prolific author. He gathered and explained the writings of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, the Vilna Gaon and the Ramchal – a bridge between the world of mussar and the Torah of the Land of Israel.
566.core_concept: Arranging the treasures of Jewish thought so that every learner can reach them: Rav Kook's teaching, ethics and aggadah as an ordered body of teaching, joining Lithuanian erudition, Kabbalistic depth and national revival.

567.label: Rabbi Shlomo Carlebach
567.bio: "The dancing rabbi" – the instigator of the revolution in Jewish music in the generation of return. His melodies and his open heart brought tens of thousands closer to Judaism.
567.core_concept: Melody and story are a way into the Torah and into the Jewish heart: unconditional love and joy as the way to bring the distant near, without giving up halakha.

568.label: Judith
568.bio: The heroine of the apocryphal book named after her, who risked her life to save her people. In tradition her figure became linked to the miracle of Chanukah.
568.core_concept: One must act within nature and history out of complete trust in God, without confining salvation to a time and place, and without waiting idly for a miracle.

569.label: Josel of Rosheim
569.bio: The great intercessor of Ashkenazi Jewry before Emperor Charles V. His "Sefer HaMikneh" is a personal testimony to leadership in a generation of decrees and the Reformation.
569.core_concept: Defending the communities is a religious duty: intercession before the emperor and the authorities, resting on rabbinic learning, moral discipline and legal expertise.

570.label: Jacob Our Father
570.bio: The chosen of the patriarchs and father of the twelve tribes. "A plain man, dwelling in tents", who went down to Egypt and laid the foundation of the house of Israel.
570.core_concept: 'You will give truth to Jacob': truth and integrity tested in exile and in struggle, from which the house of Israel was built, twelve tribes that are one people.

571.label: Isaac Our Father
571.bio: The second of the patriarchs. He was bound on the altar on Mount Moriah, and dug anew the wells of his father – continuing the way in the Land.
571.core_concept: Strength of devotion and perseverance: readiness to be bound on the altar, prayer in the field, and continuing his father's way in the Land by digging his wells anew.

572.label: Isaiah the Prophet
572.bio: One of the greatest of the literary prophets. His prophecies of destruction and consolation – "Comfort, comfort my people" – accompany Israel in every generation.
572.core_concept: Destruction is not the last word: from the same prophet came the rebuke of society's wrongs and the promise of consolation and redemption, for Israel and for all the nations.

573.label: Mahari Berab (Rabbi Yaakov Berab)
573.bio: The greatest sage of Safed in his generation and the initiator of the renewal of semikhah (1538) as a step towards hastening redemption – a move that ignited the great controversy with the sages of Jerusalem.
573.core_concept: Halakha is a living instrument meant to serve redemption: renewing semikhah and the Sanhedrin in Safed, to give the people back sovereign halakhic authority and restore its dignity after the Expulsion.

574.label: Moses Our Teacher
574.bio: Master of the prophets and receiver of the Torah at Sinai. He brought Israel out of Egypt, received the Tablets and handed the Torah to all Israel – the head of the chain of tradition.
574.core_concept: Moses received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on to Joshua (Avot 1:1).

575.label: Ezra the Scribe
575.bio: The renewer of the Torah in Israel at the start of the Second Temple period. He brought the exiles up from Babylon and established the public reading of the Torah – "Ezra was worthy that the Torah should have been given through him".
575.core_concept: The nation's survival depends not only on territory and government but on the book and on learning: Ezra turned the Torah from a closed code into the living foundation of daily life, so that wherever there is a Jew there will be a book, a language and a community.

576.label: Rav Huna
576.bio: The pillar of the second generation of Babylonian Amoraim and head of the Sura yeshiva for forty years. In monetary law the halakha follows him in most of his disputes.
576.core_concept: Torah, leadership and social justice as one whole: outstanding learning together with firmness in judgement, public humility, and wealth used for acts of kindness and the public good.

577.label: Rabbi Abun the Great
577.bio: One of the founders of the early rabbinic community on the Rhine. One of those who laid the foundation for the Torah culture of early Ashkenaz, generations before Rabbenu Gershom.
577.core_concept: The foundation of Ashkenaz's line of Torah: the study house and the family he established in the Rhineland created the setting from which Rashi's teachers came, and laid the groundwork for early Ashkenaz's Talmud commentary, liturgical poetry and esoteric teaching.

578.label: Rabbi Tarfon
578.bio: One of the great Tannaim of Yavne, a kohen who served in the Temple. Rabbi Akiva's disputant and friend; "The day is short and the work is great".
578.core_concept: A bridge between the Temple that was destroyed and the study house that was being built: keeping the priesthood and its gifts after the Destruction and using them for charity, rulings that ease the public's burden, and Torah study that must lead to action.

579.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi (Rihal)
579.bio: One of the great poets of Spain and the thinker of the "Kuzari". His poetry of longing for Zion – "My heart is in the East and I am at the edge of the West" – accompanies the nation; at the end of his life he set out for the Land of Israel.
579.core_concept: Faith is not a cold logical conclusion but prophetic experience and a whole life, bound inseparably to the people of Israel, the Land of Israel and the Hebrew language.

580.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
580.bio: The editor of the Mishnah, who sealed the age of the Tannaim. He united the traditions of the Oral Torah into one authoritative work, and combined greatness in Torah with wealth and leadership before Rome.
580.core_concept: Editing the Mishnah – the first sealing of the Oral Torah.

581.label: Rabbi Yaakov HaKohen (the Kabbalist)
581.bio: One of the first kabbalists of Castile, one of the fathers of the "Kabbalah of the Kohen brothers". His works on the letters and the Chariot preceded the Zohar and influenced it.
581.core_concept: A path to the hidden through personal vision and combinations of letters; and from it the teaching of the 'left emanation', a map of the forces of evil, which deeply influenced the Zohar.

582.label: Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi (the Rif)
582.bio: The greatest halakhic authority of the generation between the Geonim and the Rishonim. "The Halakhot of the Rif" distilled the Talmud into halakhic rulings and served as a cornerstone of the Shulchan Arukh.
582.core_concept: Halakha requires selection, distillation and decision: the Rif condensed the Babylonian Talmud into practical rulings, made the Bavli the highest source and set the rule that the law follows the later authorities, and so put halakha within reach of every rabbinic decisor.

583.label: Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi (Segan Leviah)
583.bio: One of the heads of the yeshivot of the Lotharingian lands and one of Rashi's principal teachers in Worms. One of the shapers of the early Ashkenazi tradition of study.
583.core_concept: Torah leadership that combines authority, humility and halakhic precision.

584.label: Rabbi Yishmael (ben Elisha)
584.bio: A father of the world and the master of the thirteen rules by which the Torah is expounded. Rabbi Akiva's great disputant on the ways of midrash – "the Torah speaks in human language".
584.core_concept: 'The Torah speaks in human language': systematic, reasoned interpretation through the thirteen principles, avoiding needless stringency, together with joining Torah to a worldly occupation and compassion for Israel's poor.

585.label: Rabbi Levi ben Chaviv (the Maharalbach)
585.bio: Rabbi of Jerusalem and the great opponent of the renewal of semikhah. His "Kuntres HaSemikhah" decided the famous halakhic controversy with the sages of Safed.
585.core_concept: Sovereign halakhic authority cannot be set up by one centre alone: renewing semikhah requires the consent of all the sages of the Land of Israel, to preserve the unity of the people and the Hebrew calendar.

586.label: Rabbi Moshe Alashkar (Maharam Alashkar)
586.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities after the Expulsion from Spain. He survived a sinking ship, served as a judge in Egypt and at the end of his life went up to Jerusalem.
586.core_concept: Balance in a time of crisis: complete loyalty to the rulings of the Rishonim alongside a defence of the Rambam's rationalism, to give wandering Spanish Jewry a stable framework of law and thought.

587.label: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov
587.bio: A grandson of the Baal Shem Tov and author of "Degel Machaneh Ephraim" – one of the earliest and most faithful sources of his great grandfather's teaching.
587.core_concept: Joining mystical revelation to the repair of the soul in daily life: the teaching of the Baal Shem Tov, the kavanot of the Ari and a deep understanding of the human soul, as inner service of God.

588.label: Rabbi Moshe of Coucy (the Semag)
588.bio: One of the Tosafists and author of "Sefer Mitzvot Gadol" – the great halakhic code of French Jewry. He travelled among the communities of Spain and Ashkenaz as a preacher and awakener.
588.core_concept: Preserving the Oral Torah after the burning of the Talmud: an ordered code of the 613 commandments combining Talmud, rulings, aggadah and ethics, and a call to the public to keep the commandments in deed and in conduct.

589.label: Rabbi Nathan of Breslov (of Nemirov)
589.bio: The great student and scribe of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov. He wrote down his teachings and founded the tradition of hitbodedut and prayer – "Likkutei Tefillot".
589.core_concept: For the master's prophetic fire to warm later generations, it must be poured into vessels of language, law and community; prayer and hope are the answer to despair.

590.label: Rabbi Raphael Baruch Toledano
590.bio: Head of the rabbinical court of Meknes and author of a "Kitzur Shulchan Arukh" for Sephardim. His poem "Eshtachaveh Apayim Artzah" is sung throughout the Eastern diaspora.
590.core_concept: True spiritual leadership does not shut itself away in the study house: alongside rulings and poetry, care for the poor, the orphan and the dignity of the weak, and keeping the Torah heritage of Moroccan Jewry alive in Israel too.

591.label: Rabban Gamliel of Yavne
591.bio: The leader of Israel after the destruction. He fortified the authority of the patriarchate and the unity of halakha in the generation of rebuilding at Yavne.
591.core_concept: The nation's unity after the Destruction requires central authority and uniform halakha: a fixed prayer, one calendar and the Passover Seder as a 'small sanctuary' in every home, together with humility and care for the weak.

592.label: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
592.bio: The rescuer of the Torah in the generation of the destruction. He left besieged Jerusalem and asked, "Give me Yavne and its sages" – and so secured the continuation of the Oral Torah after the destruction of the Temple.
592.core_concept: Give me Yavne and its sages.

593.label: Rebecca Our Matriarch
593.bio: The second of the matriarchs. With divine inspiration she saw her sons' destinies and decided the continuation of the covenant's way – "the elder shall serve the younger".
593.core_concept: Prophetic foresight and responsibility for the nation's future: Rebecca decided that the blessing would go to Jacob, and taught that a Jew's inner essence matters more than his outer garment.

594.label: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki)
594.bio: The greatest of Israel's commentators. His commentary on the Torah and the Talmud – clear, concise and close to the plain sense – opened the gates of study to every generation; without it no page of Gemara is learned.
594.core_concept: The plain sense of Scripture – a commentary every student can enter.

595.label: King Solomon
595.bio: The wisest of all men and builder of the First Temple. He wrote Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.
595.core_concept: Wisdom is a gift from God that obliges the king: Solomon asked for an understanding heart to judge the people, built the House for God's name, and wrote down his wisdom for all generations.

596.label: Samuel the Prophet
596.bio: The last of the judges and the greatest prophet after Moses. He established the monarchy in Israel and anointed Saul and David.
596.core_concept: Leadership as a mission, not as rule: Samuel went round the towns of Israel to judge the people, prayed for them, and handed leadership over to the monarchy without giving up the authority of prophecy.

597.label: Shmuel HaNagid
597.bio: Vizier of Granada, general, poet and halakhic authority – a symbol of the Golden Age of Spain. His "Introduction to the Talmud" is studied to this day.
597.core_concept: 'Torah and greatness in one place': statecraft, generalship, poetry, grammar and halakhic rulings joined in one person, with political power used to strengthen the Torah and those who study it.

598.label: Rabbenu Asher ben Yechiel (the Rosh)
598.bio: Born in Ashkenaz around 1250, the outstanding student of the Maharam of Rothenburg and leader of German Jewry after his teacher's death in captivity. Because of persecution he left Germany in 1303, and in 1305 he was appointed rabbi of the community and head of the yeshiva in Toledo. There he merged the dialectic of the Tosafists with Spanish ruling, and wrote "Piskei HaRosh", "Tosafot HaRosh" and "Orchot Chaim".
598.core_concept: Bringing the Ashkenazi tradition of study to Spain and creating a halakhic synthesis that made him one of the three "pillars of instruction" on which the Shulchan Arukh rests.

599.label: Rabbi Isaiah HaLevi Horowitz (the Holy Shelah)
599.bio: Born in Prague in 1558, he served in the rabbinates of Dubno, Ostroh, Posen, Kraków, Vienna and Frankfurt; in the expulsion from Frankfurt (1614–1615) he went into exile together with his community. In 1621 he went up to the Land of Israel, served as rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Jerusalem, was imprisoned by the governor Ibn Farukh, and died in Tiberias in 1630.
599.core_concept: "Shnei Luchot HaBrit" unites halakha, Kabbalah and ethics into one Torah encyclopedia that organises Jewish life around holiness, intention and educating the coming generations.

600.label: Rabbi Avraham ben HaRambam
600.bio: The Rambam's only son, born in Fustat in 1186 and appointed Nagid of the Jews of Egypt, Syria and the Land of Israel at eighteen, after his father's death in 1204. He led the community for thirty-three years, defended his father's teaching in controversies, and wrote "HaMaspik LeOvdei HaShem" and the responsa collected in "Birkat Avraham". He died in 1237 at the age of 51.
600.core_concept: "Rational piety": combining Maimonidean philosophy with ways of abstinence, intention and devotion, from the position that careful observance of the commandments and mystical devotion complement each other.

601.label: Rabbenu Chizkiyah da Silva (the Pri Chadash)
601.bio: Born in Livorno in 1656, he went up to Jerusalem, where he joined the "Beit Yaakov" yeshiva and worked to establish the Beit Yaakov (Pereira) yeshiva with the help of the magnate Jacob Pereira. In 1688 he went to Europe as an emissary of the Sages and printed his book "Pri Chadash", which stirred a sharp controversy and a ban in Egypt. He died on 28 Kislev at only 39.
601.core_concept: Halakhic boldness: returning to clarify the sugya from the source and openly criticising the rulings of earlier authorities, alongside establishing Jerusalem as a world centre of Torah.

602.label: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Abba Mari (the Ba'al ha-Ittur)
602.bio: Born in 1122, he worked in Marseille in Provence until his death in 1193. His work "Sefer HaIttur" organises the halakhic knowledge of his generation in a systematic and innovative structure, combining loyalty to the teaching of the Geonim with original and bold interpretive tools.
602.core_concept: Halakhic architecture: organising halakha as a systematic legal system bridging the scholarship of Muslim Spain and the yeshivot of northern France and Ashkenaz.

603.label: Rabbi Yaakov ibn Habib (Ein Yaakov)
603.bio: A revered head of a yeshiva in Castile who was expelled from Spain in 1492, escaped from Portugal after the forced conversion decree of 1497 and led the community of exiles in Salonica. He wrote "Ein Yaakov", a collection of the aggadot of the Talmud with a commentary, and a commentary on the "Arba'ah Turim" that Rabbi Yosef Karo had before him when writing the "Beit Yosef". He died in Salonica in 1516, and his son the Maharalbach completed his work.
603.core_concept: Rebuilding faith after the catastrophe through the aggadot of the Sages: aggadah as a spiritual foundation and a source of hope for a generation of exiles who had lost their physical world.

604.label: Rabbi Yaakov ben Yakar
604.bio: A student of Rabbenu Gershom, Light of the Exile, who continued his leadership of the yeshiva in Mainz after his death in 1028, and Rashi's principal teacher. He was born around 990 and died in 1064, and was buried in the old cemetery of Mainz.
604.core_concept: Establishing the tradition of study and correcting the text of the Talmud in early Ashkenaz – a work that reached its peak with his student Rashi.

605.label: Rabbi Yosei ben Halafta
605.bio: A Tanna of the fourth generation, born in Tzippori to Rabbi Chalafta and a student of his principal teacher, Rabbi Akiva. His student Issi ben Yehuda coined the rule "Rabbi Yosei – his reasoning is with him", and his reasoned rulings became decisive in almost every dispute. He wrote "Seder Olam", the first systematic Hebrew chronicle of biblical chronology.
605.core_concept: Reasoning as a source of authority: clear, reasoned ruling as a tool for mending a divided people after the destruction, and chronological order as an anchor for national memory.

606.label: Mordechai the Jew
606.bio: Leader of the Jews of Persia in the days of Ahasuerus, a member of the Sanhedrin and of the Men of the Great Assembly, called "Mordechai Bilshan" for his command of languages – which enabled him to uncover the plot of Bigthan and Teresh. He worked to fortify Jewish life both in the Diaspora and in Jerusalem, and his figure is read as a bridge between the age of prophecy and the beginning of the age of halakha and the leadership of the Sages.
606.core_concept: Leadership that combines uncompromising religious devotion with political sophistication: translating God's will into the languages of political reality without losing the sacred core.

607.label: Isaac Samuel Reggio (the Yashar of Gorizia)
607.bio: Born in Gorizia in 1784, he learned Talmud and grammar from his father alongside the sciences and European languages. He initiated and founded the Rabbinical College in Padua, opened in 1829 as the first modern rabbinical seminary in Europe, where Shadal taught. In his book "HaTorah VehaPhilosophia" he sought to reconcile reason and science with faith, and in his later writings he criticised Kabbalah and accepted rabbinic authority.
607.core_concept: Reconciling reason and faith: rabbinic leadership requires both Torah knowledge and general education, hence the need for a modern, institutional rabbinic training.

608.label: Rabbi Yosef Dov HaLevi Soloveitchik (the Rav)
608.bio: A continuer of the Brisk method, a philosopher and head of a yeshiva who became a central figure of Modern Orthodoxy in the United States. He combined analytic halakhic scholarship with modern philosophy and dealt with the tension between human creativity, science and society on one side and covenant, prayer and faith on the other.
608.core_concept: There is no need to resolve every tension between tradition and modernity. The believer can live with full force in both worlds – act, create and master reality, and at the same time stand in humility, covenant and responsibility before God.

609.label: Rabbi Yirmiyahu Chachiashvili
609.bio: The son and successor of Chacham Chaim Eliashvili (Chachiashvili), rabbi of Kutaisi – "the Jerusalem of Georgia" – who in 1924 led the struggle to recover the synagogues from the Soviet authorities. Rabbi Yirmiyahu led the community under the communist regime, moved to Israel and became a spiritual beacon for Georgian Jews in Ashdod, while carefully preserving the Georgian custom.
609.core_concept: Activist rabbinate: the rabbi as the community's representative, responsible not only for teaching but also for the legal and public struggle over the community's institutions and synagogues.

610.label: Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka Schneerson
610.bio: The daughter of the Rebbe Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn and wife of the Lubavitcher Rebbe. Born in 1901 near Lubavitch, she took part in the underground work to preserve Judaism in the Soviet Union and in the efforts around her father's arrest in 1927, and escaped with her husband from occupied Europe until they reached New York in 1941. Her testimony in the books trial – "My father and the books belong to the Hasidim" – decided the case. She passed away on 22 Shevat 5748 (1988).
610.core_concept: Extreme modesty and concealment alongside spiritual resilience and public responsibility: the tzaddik and his possessions belong to all the Hasidim, not to an individual.

611.label: Geula Cohen
611.bio: Born in Tel Aviv in 1925, she joined the Lehi underground in late 1943, where she was "the voice of Lehi" in its broadcasts. She served in the Knesset for nineteen consecutive years until 1992, left the Likud in 1978 over the Camp David Accords, and founded the Tehiya movement with Yuval Ne'eman. She established the National Midrasha and the Uri Zvi Greenberg Heritage House, won the Israel Prize in 2003 and died in 2019.
611.core_concept: Turning the broadcast and written word into a tool of national struggle, and linking the heritage of the undergrounds with the enterprise of settlement and Zionist education.

612.label: Rabbi Moses Mendelssohn (Rambeman)
612.bio: A thinker who stood on the seam between the world of halakha and the values of the 18th-century Enlightenment. He wrote the "Biur" project on the Bible to bridge the linguistic and cultural gap of the Jews of his time, and in his book "Jerusalem" he proposed separating religion and state and defined Judaism as a religion of practical commandments, not of compelled belief.
612.core_concept: Judaism as a religion based on practical commandments, not on compelled belief – opening a window to modernity that also raised fears of assimilation.

613.label: Leah Our Matriarch
613.bio: The wife of Jacob and mother of six of the tribes of Israel and of Dinah. The Sages linked her "tender eyes" to weeping and prayer over her fate, and the birth of Judah to the move from longing for love to gratitude; in the teaching of mystery she is identified with the covered world and inwardness.
613.core_concept: Prayer can change the course of life, and gratitude grows from recognising that one has received more than could be taken for granted; Leah embodies the hidden power from which Levi and Judah grow – priesthood and kingship.

614.label: Solika Hachuel
614.bio: A Jewish girl from Morocco who was executed in the 19th century after refusing to convert to Islam, and became a symbol of sanctifying God's name. She held firmly to her Jewish identity until her death, and her memory is kept to this day in poems and in prayers at her grave in the cemetery of Fez.
614.core_concept: Holding to Jewish identity to the point of self-sacrifice, and modesty as a tool of holiness in the face of death.

615.label: Rav Nachman bar Papa
615.bio: A Babylonian Amora mentioned in halakhic sugyot and in an aggadah about a prayer that brought rain and made seeds sprout. The completion tradition counts him among the ten sons of Rav Papa, although the exact identification and lineage raise a chronological difficulty.
615.core_concept: Reality demands human participation on two planes: precision in the rights and duties between people, and prayer that turns a person from an onlooker into an active partner within the world.

616.label: Gedaliah ben Ahikam
616.bio: The leader of the remnant of Judah, appointed by the Babylonians after the destruction of Jerusalem, who tried to renew agricultural and public life in the Land. His murder by Ishmael son of Nethaniah wrecked the attempt at rebuilding and led many to flee to Egypt.
616.core_concept: Responsible leadership must distinguish between accepting a rumour as truth and taking care in the face of real danger; his story teaches how far internal zealotry can extinguish a possibility of national recovery.

617.label: Rabbi Yisrael Yitzchak Besançon
617.bio: A rabbi, Breslov Hasid, writer, painter and composer who joined the world of modern art with the service of God and the teaching of Rabbi Nachman. In Tel Aviv he founded the "Shir Chadash" community and developed a language of emotional coping, breathing, creativity and hitbodedut.
617.core_concept: A deep tradition can speak to modern man also through colour, sound and breath; creativity and emotional sensitivity are not a substitute for the service of God but can become tools of prayer, growth and connection.

618.label: Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg (the Tzitz Eliezer)
618.bio: One of the great halakhic authorities of the last generation and a pioneer of modern medical halakha. In the 22-volume responsa "Tzitz Eliezer" he clarified medical and technological questions by studying scientific reality, and in "Hilchot Medinah" he dealt with sovereignty, the army and public systems in a Jewish state.
618.core_concept: Halakha does not retreat before a new reality: to rule correctly one must first understand the scientific and social facts, and then apply the principles of the Torah to them out of responsibility for life, the person and the public.

619.label: Rabbi Achai bar Pappa
619.bio: An Amora of the third generation who was active in Babylonia and the Land of Israel and is mentioned in halakhic sugyot that call for fine distinctions between practical situations. His name is included in the tradition of "the ten sons of Rav Papa", although chronology shows that he lived generations before the famous Rav Papa.
619.core_concept: Halakha works within a complex human reality: precise definitions, sensitivity to the psychology of the parties and an understanding of the conditions of the time are part of the law itself. His figure also shows how a tradition of memory can bind together sages from different periods.

620.label: Rabbi Hanan Porat
620.bio: A Torah scholar, educator, settlement activist and member of the Knesset who was one of the prominent figures of religious Zionism after the Six-Day War. He worked to re-establish Kfar Etzion, to found Torah institutions and to join the study of the Bible, the Land, society and public action.
620.core_concept: "The secret of grafting" seeks to join Joseph and Judah – building the Land, the army and society with Torah, holiness and spirit. The Torah is tested by its ability to become a practical life of kindness, national responsibility and connection between the parts of the people.

621.label: Rabbi Menachem Recanati
621.bio: One of the great kabbalists of Italy, who joined Spanish Kabbalah, the traditions of the Ashkenazi Pietists and the Italian world of halakha. In his writings he included hundreds of quotations from the Zohar even before it was printed, explained its language and helped make it a central source of authority in the world of Kabbalah.
621.core_concept: Halakha and Kabbalah are two storeys of the same action: halakha defines the deed in the revealed world, and Kabbalah explains its meaning in the hidden world. Prayer, letters and commandments become part of a spiritual system of repair and influence.

622.label: Rabbi Yehuda Leib HaLevi Ashlag (the Baal HaSulam)
622.bio: One of the great interpreters of Kabbalah in the modern era. In "Talmud Eser HaSefirot" he arranged the writings of the Ari into a method of study, and in the "Sulam" commentary he made the Zohar accessible. Alongside this he developed a social thought centred on the move from the will to receive for oneself to responsibility, mutual guarantee and giving.
622.core_concept: Spiritual repair does not stay in the upper worlds: changing the intention of the individual is meant to radiate onto the structure of society too. Love of others, mutual guarantee and responsibility are, in his eyes, the social translation of the kabbalistic idea of giving.
